berakhot-3a-11-13.note: Rabbi Yosei recalls entering a ruin in Jerusalem to pray. Elijah came and guarded the entrance until he finished, then greeted him and asked why he had gone in. To pray, Rabbi Yosei said. Elijah said he should have prayed on the road; Rabbi Yosei feared travelers would interrupt him; Elijah said he should then have said the short prayer. Rabbi Yosei learned three things: not to enter a ruin, that one may pray on the road, and that on the road one says a short prayer. Elijah asked what he had heard there. A Heavenly voice cooing like a dove, he said: Woe, that I destroyed My house, burned My Temple and exiled My children. Elijah said it cries so three times a day, and that when Israel praises God's name in the synagogue, God laments the children exiled from their father's table.
berakhot-3a-11-13.why: Rav, as quoted just before, taught that God roars like a lion at each watch of the night over the Temple's destruction. Rabbi Yosei's account bears out that lament, and the Gemara then turns to why one may not enter a ruin.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Tells the story; he went into the ruin to pray.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who guards the entrance and then questions and teaches Rabbi Yosei.

terms.meaning: A short form of the central daily prayer, set for someone who cannot concentrate on the full version, such as a traveler on the road.
A voice from Heaven, heard by people, that speaks for God.
A prayer said in the synagogue; the congregation answers 'May His great name be blessed'.

berakhot-5b-9-9.note: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba fell ill. Rabbi Yoḥanan came to visit and asked him: Is your suffering dear to you? Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said: Neither the suffering nor its reward. Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Give me your hand. He gave him his hand, and Rabbi Yoḥanan raised him up.
berakhot-5b-9-9.why: The Gemara is weighing which sufferings count as 'afflictions of love', sent by God out of love and bringing reward. Here a sick man says he wants neither the suffering nor its reward.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba
people.about: The sick man; the translation calls him Rabbi Yoḥanan's student.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Visits him and raises him from his sickbed.

terms.meaning: The discussion holds that suffering accepted with love brings reward from God. Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba would rather be spared both.

berakhot-5b-10-10.note: Rabbi Yoḥanan fell ill. Rabbi Ḥanina came to visit and asked him: Is your suffering dear to you? Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Neither the suffering nor its reward. Rabbi Ḥanina said: Give me your hand. He gave him his hand, and Rabbi Ḥanina raised him up.
berakhot-5b-10-10.why: It mirrors the story just told, in which Rabbi Yoḥanan healed his own student. The Gemara asks why he could not raise himself, and answers that a prisoner cannot free himself from prison.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The sick man here, though in the story before he healed another.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: Visits Rabbi Yoḥanan and raises him from his sickbed.

berakhot-5b-13-15.note: Rabbi Elazar fell ill, and Rabbi Yoḥanan came to visit. Rabbi Elazar was lying in a dark room; Rabbi Yoḥanan bared his arm, and light shone from it. He saw Rabbi Elazar crying and asked why. If over Torah he had not learned enough, he said, it matters only that the heart is turned to Heaven; if over poverty, not everyone gets two tables; if over children, here is the bone of my tenth son. Rabbi Elazar said: I am crying over this beauty of yours that will rot in the earth. Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Over that you surely should cry, and both of them wept. Meanwhile Rabbi Yoḥanan asked if his suffering was dear to him. Neither it nor its reward, he said. Give me your hand, said Rabbi Yoḥanan, and he raised him up.
berakhot-5b-13-15.why: It completes a series of sickbed visits in a discussion of 'afflictions of love'. Rabbi Yoḥanan's consolations go over the sufferings the Gemara has been sorting, and the bone of his tenth son was quoted earlier when it asked whether losing children counts.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: The sick man, who weeps over Rabbi Yoḥanan's beauty; the translation calls him Rabbi Yoḥanan's student.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Visits, consoles and weeps with Rabbi Elazar, then raises him up.

terms.meaning: The translation explains this as wealth and Torah learning together; not everyone is granted both.

terms.term: the bone of my tenth son
terms.meaning: Earlier in the discussion the Gemara explains that Rabbi Yoḥanan lost ten children and kept a small bone of the tenth, which he showed to console others.

berakhot-5b-16-19.note: Four hundred barrels of Rav Huna's wine turned to vinegar. Rav Yehuda, brother of Rav Sala the Pious, came with the Sages (some say Rav Adda bar Ahava with the Sages) and told him to examine his deeds. Am I suspect in your eyes? he asked. They answered: Is God suspect of judging without justice? Rav Huna said: If anyone has heard something against me, say it. They had heard he did not give his tenant farmer his share of the vine cuttings. He steals everything from me, said Rav Huna. They answered with the saying: steal from a thief and you too get a taste of theft. Rav Huna took it on himself to give the share. Some say the vinegar turned back into wine; some say the price of vinegar rose until it sold at the price of wine.
berakhot-5b-16-19.why: It follows a series of stories about suffering. Here the loss is treated as a sign to examine one's conduct, and once the wrong is put right the loss is undone.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage whose wine soured and who is asked to examine his deeds.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Brother of Rav Sala the Pious; he and the Sages visit Rav Huna.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: Named in another version as the visitor in place of Rav Yehuda.

terms.meaning: A man who works another's land in return for a share of what it produces. The translation explains he was also owed a share of the vine cuttings.

berakhot-6b-19-19.note: A man prayed behind the synagogue without turning to face it. Elijah passed by and saw him, and appeared to him as an Arab. He said: Is this how you stand before your Master? Elijah drew a sword and killed him.
berakhot-6b-19-19.why: Rav Huna has just said that one who prays behind the synagogue is called wicked, and Abaye limited this to one who does not turn his face toward it. This man is exactly that case.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who appears to the man as an Arab and kills him.

terms.meaning: As Rav Huna explains just before, standing outside and facing away while the congregation inside faces the other way, which looks like contempt for the synagogue.
God, before whom one stands in prayer.

berakhot-7a-3-3.note: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha recalls that he once entered the innermost sanctum of the Temple to offer incense. He saw Akatriel Ya, the Lord of Hosts, seated on a high and exalted throne, who said: Yishmael, My son, bless Me. He answered: May it be Your will that Your mercy overcome Your anger, that Your mercy prevail over Your other attributes, that You deal with Your children with mercy, and that You go beyond the letter of the law for them. God nodded His head. The Gemara draws the lesson that one should not take even an ordinary person's blessing lightly.
berakhot-7a-3-3.why: Rav has just taught, as Rav Zutra bar Tovia reports, that God Himself prays in these very words, asking that His mercy overcome His anger. Rabbi Yishmael's blessing echoes that prayer.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha
people.about: The High Priest, according to the translation, who enters to offer incense and is asked to bless God.

people.name: Akatriel Ya, the Lord of Hosts
people.about: A name for God; He asks Rabbi Yishmael for a blessing and nods in acceptance.

terms.meaning: The Holy of Holies, the innermost room of the Temple in Jerusalem. The translation adds that the High Priest entered it on Yom Kippur to burn incense.

terms.term: beyond the letter of the law
terms.meaning: Acting more generously than strict justice requires.

berakhot-7a-18-18.note: A heretic who lived near Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi tormented him with challenges about verses of the Bible. One day Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi took a rooster, set it between the legs of his bed and watched it, planning to curse the man when the moment of God's anger came. When that moment came, he was asleep. He concluded that it is not proper to do such a thing, since it is written: His mercy is over all His works.
berakhot-7a-18-18.why: Abaye has just said that the moment of God's anger can be known by a rooster: its crest turns white with no red streaks. The story shows a Sage trying to use that sign, and the Gemara adds a verse that punishment is not good even for the righteous.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage who plans to curse his tormentor and falls asleep at the moment he waited for.

terms.meaning: Someone who rejects the Sages' teaching; this one kept challenging Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi over verses.
A brief moment each day when, the discussion says, God is angry, so a curse spoken then might take effect.

berakhot-7b-26-27.note: Rabbi Yitzhak asked Rav Nahman why he had not come to the synagogue to pray. Rav Nahman said he was too weak. Rabbi Yitzhak suggested he gather ten men at home to pray; Rav Nahman said that would be too much of a burden on them. Then let the congregation send a messenger to tell you when they are praying, Rabbi Yitzhak said, so you can pray at the same moment. When Rav Nahman asked why he was going to such lengths, Rabbi Yitzhak quoted Rabbi Yohanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai: the 'time of favor' in the Psalm is the time when the congregation prays.
berakhot-7b-26-27.why: The Gemara has been quoting Rabbi Yohanan's teachings in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai; this exchange introduces another of them, and other Sages then add their own verses showing the special power of praying with a community.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel who urges Rav Nahman to pray together with the congregation.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage and judge, here too weak to come to synagogue.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The leading Sage of the Land of Israel in the third century, quoted by Rabbi Yitzhak.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: A great second-century Sage, student of Rabbi Akiva, whose teaching Rabbi Yohanan passes on.

terms.meaning: A prayer quorum, called a minyan: the ten adult men needed for communal prayer.
A phrase from Psalms 69:14, read here as a moment when God is especially ready to accept prayer.

berakhot-8b-9-9.note: Rav Pappa went to visit an Aramean woman. She brought out a bed and told him to sit. He said he would not sit until she lifted the bedding. She lifted it, and they found a dead baby there. The translation explains that had he sat, he would have been blamed for killing the child. From this the Sages said it is forbidden to sit on an Aramean woman's bed.
berakhot-8b-9-9.why: Rava has just advised his sons not to sit on the bed of an Aramean woman, and the Gemara gives three readings of his words. This incident explains the literal reading.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who refuses to sit until the bed is uncovered.

terms.meaning: A non-Jewish woman, as the translation explains.

berakhot-9a-3-3.note: A pair of Sages got drunk at the wedding of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's son. The translation explains that they fell asleep before saying the evening Shema and woke after dawn. They came before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who said: Rabbi Shimon is worthy of being relied on in a pressing situation.
berakhot-9a-3-3.why: A ruling had been reported in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's name that the law follows Rabbi Shimon, who lets the evening Shema be said just before sunrise. Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef said he never said so outright; it was inferred from this incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage at whose son's wedding the two got drunk; they ask him what to do.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The Sage whose lenient view Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi lets them rely on.

terms.meaning: The central declaration of faith ('Hear, O Israel'), said each evening and morning within set times.
Under hardship or after the fact. A lenient view relied on only then is not the rule for ordinary cases.

berakhot-10a-1-3.note: Some hooligans in Rabbi Meir's neighborhood caused him a great deal of anguish, and he prayed that they would die. His wife Berurya challenged him: the verse he relied on says "Let sins cease from the land", not sinners, and it ends "and the wicked will be no more", which can only mean the wicked stop being wicked. Pray instead, she told him, that they repent. Rabbi Meir prayed for mercy on them, and they repented.
berakhot-10a-1-3.why: The discussion has been reading the opening psalms and David's attitude to the wicked. Berurya's reading turns a verse about the end of the wicked into a hope for their repentance, and the Gemara goes on to another example of her sharp reading of scripture.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage troubled by hooligans in his neighborhood, who first prays for their death.

people.name: Berurya
people.about: Rabbi Meir's wife, who corrects his reading of the verse.

berakhot-11a-14-15.note: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya were dining together, Rabbi Yishmael reclining and Rabbi Elazar sitting upright. When the time for the evening Shema came, Rabbi Elazar reclined and Rabbi Yishmael sat up. Rabbi Elazar took offense and told a parable of a man who grows his beard only to spite those who shave: whatever I do, you do the opposite. Rabbi Yishmael answered that he had acted as Beit Hillel rule and Rabbi Elazar as Beit Shammai rule, and that he feared the students would see Rabbi Elazar and fix the law that way for generations.
berakhot-11a-14-15.why: A baraita reports Beit Hillel's ruling that Shema may be said in any position, and brings this incident to show it in practice. The Gemara then asks why Rabbi Yishmael needed his second reason, the fear about the students.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A Sage who sits up for the evening Shema to show it need not be said reclining.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Rabbi Yishmael's dining companion, who reclines for Shema and is offended when Rabbi Yishmael sits up.

terms.meaning: The declaration of faith beginning "Hear, O Israel", which Jews recite every evening and morning.
Two early schools of Sages who disagree on many rulings. The law usually follows Beit Hillel.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first great written collection of Jewish law.

berakhot-11a-20-21.note: Beit Hillel told Beit Shammai of a time when the elders of both schools visited Rabbi Yoḥanan ben HaḤoranit during Sukkot. They found him with his head and most of his body inside the sukka and his table inside the house, and, Beit Hillel said, no one said a word to him. Beit Shammai replied that this proves nothing: the elders did tell him that if this was his habit, he had never in his life fulfilled the mitzva of sukka.
berakhot-11a-20-21.why: Rav Yosef holds that one who follows Beit Shammai on Shema has done nothing at all. He cites this dispute: Beit Shammai held that someone who ignored their ruling had not fulfilled the mitzva, and since the law follows Beit Hillel, the same applies to those who follow Beit Shammai.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben HaḤoranit
people.about: The man the elders of both schools visited, found sitting partly outside his sukka.

terms.meaning: The temporary hut in which Jews eat and live during the festival of Sukkot.
A commandment of the Torah or of the Sages.
Two early schools of Sages who disagree on many rulings. The law usually follows Beit Hillel.

berakhot-11b-20-20.note: Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Yosei bar Abba happened to visit a certain place, and the people there asked them what the "single blessing" in a certain mishna was. They had no answer ready. They went and asked Rav Mattana, who also had no answer. Then they asked Rav Yehuda, who told them that Shmuel said it was the blessing "An abounding love".
berakhot-11b-20-20.why: A mishna about the Temple says the priests on duty were told to recite a single blessing before Shema, without naming it. This story answers which one; the Gemara then brings Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's view that it was "Who creates light".

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: A Sage asked about the mishna while visiting a certain place.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei bar Abba
people.about: Rabbi Abba's companion on the visit.

people.name: Rav Mattana
people.about: The first Sage they asked, who had no answer.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who gave the answer, in the name of Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage whose answer Rav Yehuda reports.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the Mishna, the first great written collection of Jewish law, on which the Gemara comments.
The opening words, and so the name, of a blessing about God's love for Israel and the gift of Torah, said before the morning Shema.

berakhot-16a-2-5.note: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi were tying the wedding canopy for Rabbi Elazar. He told them he would go to the study hall in the meantime and bring them back something new. There he heard a teaching recited before Rabbi Yoḥanan: one who erred in Shema and does not know where must go back to the start of the paragraph, or to the first break, or to the first of the two verses about writing. Rabbi Yoḥanan added that if he had already begun "In order to lengthen your days", he can assume he kept to his routine. Rabbi Elazar came back and told them, and they said: Had we come only to hear this, it would have been enough.
berakhot-16a-2-5.why: The mishna has just ruled that one who erred in Shema goes back to where he erred. The story supplies the rule for one who does not know where his mistake was.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: One of the two Sages tying Rabbi Elazar's wedding canopy.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: The other Sage tying the canopy.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: The groom, who slips off to the study hall and brings back a teaching.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage in the study hall who adds his comment to the teaching.

terms.meaning: The declaration of faith beginning "Hear, O Israel", which Jews recite every evening and morning.
Here, a man in the study hall whose job was to memorize and recite teachings word for word.

berakhot-16b-10-10.note: When Rabbi Eliezer's maidservant died, his students came to comfort him. He went up to the upper floor, then into the gatehouse, then into the banquet hall, and they followed him each time. He said: I thought a hint, like lukewarm water, would be enough to burn you; now you are not burned even by boiling water. Did I not teach you that for slaves and maidservants there is no row of comforters and no mourners' blessing or consolation? Instead one says, as for a man whose ox or donkey died: May the Omnipresent replenish your loss.
berakhot-16b-10-10.why: The mishna said Rabban Gamliel accepted condolences when his servant Tavi died. A baraita rules that one does not formally comfort mourners for slaves, and this story shows Rabbi Eliezer applying that rule.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage whose maidservant died, who refuses his students' condolences.

terms.meaning: Comforters stood in a line so the mourners could pass between them and be consoled.
A name for God.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first great written collection of Jewish law.

berakhot-18a-12-13.note: Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Yonatan were walking in a cemetery, and the sky-blue string of Rabbi Yonatan's ritual fringes was dragging over the graves. Rabbi Ḥiyya told him to lift it, so the dead would not say: Tomorrow they will join us, and now they insult us. Rabbi Yonatan asked whether the dead know so much, since scripture says "the dead know nothing". Rabbi Ḥiyya told him he had not studied the verse properly: "the living" who know they will die are the righteous, who are called living even in death, like Benayahu son of Yehoyada, "son of a living man". The text does not say whether Rabbi Yonatan lifted the string.
berakhot-18a-12-13.why: The discussion has been about the respect owed to the dead, such as escorting a funeral. This exchange opens the question the Gemara pursues next: do the dead know what happens among the living?

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: A Sage who tells his companion not to insult the dead with his dragging fringes.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan
people.about: Rabbi Ḥiyya's companion, who doubts the dead know anything.

terms.meaning: Strings tied to the corners of a garment as the Torah commands; one string was dyed sky-blue.

berakhot-18b-3-3.note: The sons of Rabbi Ḥiyya went out to the villages, forgot what they had learned, and struggled to recall it. One asked whether their dead father knew of their anguish. The other answered from Job: His sons are honored yet he shall not know it. The first replied with the next verse, Only in his flesh does he feel pain, and Rabbi Yitzḥak's teaching that maggots hurt the dead like a needle in living flesh. They concluded that the dead know of their own pain but not of the pain of others.
berakhot-18b-3-3.why: The Gemara has just said the righteous are called living even in death and applied 'the dead know nothing' to the wicked; the brothers' exchange asks what the dead know, and the Gemara then challenges their answer with a story of spirits in a cemetery.

people.name: The sons of Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Two brothers who forget their learning and wonder whether their father knows

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Their dead father

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak
people.about: A Sage whose teaching about the pain of the dead one brother quotes

berakhot-18b-6-9.note: In a drought year a pious man gave a poor man a dinar on the eve of Rosh HaShana. His wife mocked him, and he went and slept in the cemetery. He heard two spirits talking: one could not roam because she was buried in a mat of reeds, so the other went and heard from behind the heavenly curtain that hail would strike crops sown in the first rainy season. He sowed in the second, and only his crops were spared. The next year he heard that blight would strike the second sowing, sowed in the first, and was spared again. His wife asked why and he told her. Soon she quarreled with the dead girl's mother and taunted her that her daughter was buried in reeds. The next year the spirits said: our words have been heard among the living.
berakhot-18b-6-9.why: The Gemara had concluded that the dead know their own pain but not that of others. This teaching is raised as a challenge, since the spirits knew what was said among the living; the Gemara answers that perhaps someone who died told them.

terms.meaning: The curtain that separates God's presence from the world; what is heard behind it is what has been decided in heaven.
The Jewish New Year, when the coming year is judged.
The rains of autumn came in stages; farmers chose which stage to sow in.

berakhot-18b-11-11.note: Ze'iri used to leave his money with his innkeeper, a woman. While he was going back and forth to the school of Rav, she died. He went after her to the cemetery and asked her where the money was. She told him to get it from beneath the door hinge in a certain place, and to tell her mother to send her comb and her tube of eyeshadow with a certain woman who would be coming there the next day.
berakhot-18b-11-11.why: The Gemara is testing whether the dead know what happens among the living, and brings this as a proof: she knew who would die tomorrow. It rejects the proof, suggesting the angel Duma, who watches over the dead, announces arrivals in advance.

people.name: Ze'iri
people.about: A Sage who goes to the grave of his innkeeper to ask where his money is.

terms.meaning: The study house of the Sage Rav, where Ze'iri was going to learn.

berakhot-18b-13-15.note: Orphans' money had been left with Shmuel's father, who died while Shmuel was away, so people called Shmuel the son of one who eats orphans' money. Shmuel went to the cemetery and asked the dead for Abba bar Abba, father of Shmuel, and was told he had gone up to the yeshiva on high. Shmuel saw his friend Levi sitting outside, barred for having upset Rabbi Afes by not attending his yeshiva. His father came, crying because Shmuel would soon join him and laughing because Shmuel was very important in this world. Shmuel said: if I am important, let them admit Levi, and they did. His father told him the money was in the millhouse, his own on top and bottom and the orphans' in the middle, so thieves or the earth would take his own first.
berakhot-18b-13-15.why: Another proof that the dead know what happens among the living: Shmuel's father knew his son would soon die. The Gemara answers that Shmuel may be different, since for so important a man they announce in advance to make room.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The son, accused of keeping orphans' money, who goes to the cemetery to ask his dead father.

people.name: Abba bar Abba
people.about: Shmuel's father, who had held the orphans' money.

people.name: Levi
people.about: Shmuel's friend, kept outside the heavenly yeshiva until Shmuel speaks for him.

people.name: Rabbi Afes
people.about: The head of a yeshiva whom Levi upset by not attending it.

terms.meaning: The academy in heaven where, in the Gemara's stories, the righteous dead study Torah.

berakhot-19a-2-2.note: Rav Pappa reported that after Mar Shmuel died, someone spoke disparagingly about him, and a reed fell from the ceiling and fractured his skull.
berakhot-19a-2-2.why: Rabbi Yitzḥak said speaking ill of the dead is like speaking about a stone, because the dead either do not know or do not care. This report challenges that; the Gemara answers that a Torah scholar is different, because God Himself upholds his honor.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who was spoken of disparagingly after his death.

berakhot-19a-9-9.note: Rabbi Yehuda insisted that Akavya ben Mahalalel was never ostracized, God forbid, since no one in all Israel matched him in wisdom, purity and fear of sin. The man who was ostracized, he said, was Elazar ben Ḥanokh, who cast doubt on the washing of the hands. When he died, the court sent word and a large stone was placed on his coffin, to teach that when someone dies under a ban, the court stones his coffin.
berakhot-19a-9-9.why: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said the Mishna has twenty-four cases where the court ostracizes someone to defend the honor of a teacher, and Rabbi Elazar found three. This is the source for one of them: one who demeans the washing of the hands.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who denies that Akavya ben Mahalalel was ostracized.

people.name: Akavya ben Mahalalel
people.about: A Sage said in another account to have been ostracized; Rabbi Yehuda says no one matched his wisdom and purity.

people.name: Elazar ben Ḥanokh
people.about: The man Rabbi Yehuda says was ostracized, for doubting the washing of the hands.

terms.meaning: A ban imposed by a court: the person is shunned by the community until the ban is lifted.
A ritual washing of the hands instituted by the Sages.

berakhot-19a-10-10.note: Ḥoni HaMe'aggel, the circle-drawer, drew a circle, stood inside it and said he would not leave until it rained, even making demands about how the rain should fall. After the rain came, Shimon ben Shataḥ sent him word: You deserve to be ostracized, and if you were not Ḥoni I would ostracize you. But what can I do? You nag God and He does your bidding, like a son who nags his father and gets his way. About you scripture says: "Your father and mother will be glad, and she who bore you will rejoice."
berakhot-19a-10-10.why: The Gemara is listing the Mishna's cases where the court ostracizes to defend honor. This is its source for the third case Rabbi Elazar found: one who is arrogant toward Heaven would ordinarily deserve the ban.

people.name: Ḥoni HaMe'aggel
people.about: The circle-drawer, who would not leave his circle until God sent rain.

people.name: Shimon ben Shataḥ
people.about: The head of the Sanhedrin, who says Ḥoni deserves a ban but cannot impose it.

terms.meaning: A ban imposed by a court: the person is shunned by the community until the ban is lifted.
The high court of the Sages.

berakhot-19a-11-11.note: Theodosius of Rome, a leader of the Jews there, started a custom for them to eat whole roasted young goats on the eve of Passover, as was done with the Passover lamb in the Temple. Shimon ben Shataḥ sent him word: If you were not Theodosius, I would ostracize you, because you are feeding Israel consecrated food outside the Temple.
berakhot-19a-11-11.why: After finding three ostracism cases, the Gemara asks whether there are more, and raises this one. It answers that this case does not count, because it comes from a baraita, not from the Mishna that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was counting.

people.name: Theodosius of Rome
people.about: The leader of the Jews of Rome, who began the custom of roasted goats on Passover eve.

people.name: Shimon ben Shataḥ
people.about: The Sage who warns Theodosius he would ban him if he were not so important.

terms.meaning: A ban imposed by a court: the person is shunned by the community until the ban is lifted.
Food from sacrifices, which may be eaten only at the Temple; roasting goats like the Passover lamb looked like eating sacrifices elsewhere.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first great written collection of Jewish law.

berakhot-20a-4-4.note: Rav Adda bar Ahava saw a woman in the market wearing a garment of wool and linen woven together, which the Torah forbids. Thinking she was Jewish, he ripped it off her. She turned out not to be Jewish, and the payment for her shame was set at four hundred zuz. He asked her name, and she said Matun. He said, punning on matan, the Aramaic for two hundred: Matun, matun, is worth four hundred zuz.
berakhot-20a-4-4.why: Rav Pappa asked Abaye why miracles happened for earlier generations and not for theirs, though they studied more. Abaye answered that the earlier Sages gave themselves wholly for the sanctification of God's name, and this incident shows that zeal.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: A Sage who tears a forbidden garment off a woman he thinks is Jewish.

people.name: Matun
people.about: The woman whose garment he tore; she was not Jewish.

terms.meaning: A silver coin.

berakhot-22a-6-6.note: Rabbi Yehuda had had a seminal emission and was walking along the riverbank with his disciples. They asked him to teach them a chapter of Hilkhot Derekh Eretz. He went down into the river, immersed, and taught them. They said: Did you not teach us that one may study Hilkhot Derekh Eretz in that state? He answered: Although I am lenient with others, I am strict with myself.
berakhot-22a-6-6.why: The Sages barred a man who had a seminal emission from studying Torah, and Sages disagree how far the ban reaches. Rabbi Yehuda allows only Hilkhot Derekh Eretz; the story shows him holding himself to more than his own ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who immerses before teaching, though his own ruling did not require it.

terms.meaning: Under a rule of the Sages, a man who has had a seminal emission is ritually impure and may not study Torah until he purifies himself with water.
Teachings on proper conduct and manners.
Dipped his whole body in natural water to become ritually pure.

berakhot-22a-7-7.note: A student was reciting hesitantly before Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira; the translation explains that he had had a seminal emission and did not want to say words of Torah plainly. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira told him: My son, open your mouth and let your words shine, for words of Torah do not become impure. As scripture says, "Is not my word like fire, says the Lord": just as fire does not become impure, words of Torah do not become impure.
berakhot-22a-7-7.why: The discussion is about how much Torah a man may study after a seminal emission. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira allows all of it, and Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak later says common practice follows him on this.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: The Sage who tells a hesitant student that Torah cannot become impure.

terms.meaning: Under a rule of the Sages, a man who has had a seminal emission is ritually impure and may not study Torah until he purifies himself with water.
In a state of ritual impurity, which bars a person or object from certain holy things until purified.

berakhot-22a-19-19.note: A man tried to persuade a woman to sin with him. She said to him: Good-for-nothing! Do you have forty se'a of water to immerse yourself in afterwards? He immediately gave up.
berakhot-22a-19-19.why: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asked why one needs a full immersion of forty se'a when nine kav poured over a person might do. Rabbi Ḥanina answers that the demanding rule is a great fence against sin, and cites this incident.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: The Sage who cites this incident.

terms.meaning: The amount of water a ritual bath must hold; a se'a is a measure of volume. Immersing in it removes impurity, here the impurity after intercourse.

berakhot-22a-22-22.note: Rabbi Zeira was sitting in a tub of water in the bathhouse and told his attendant to bring nine kav of water and pour it over him. Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba asked why he needed that, since he was already sitting in water. Rabbi Zeira answered that nine kav is like forty se'a: just as forty se'a purifies by immersion and not by pouring, nine kav purifies by pouring and not by immersion.
berakhot-22a-22-22.why: The Sages are debating how a man becomes pure after a seminal emission: immersion in forty se'a, in a heated bath, or nine kav poured over him. Rabbi Zeira's act shows how the nine-kav method must be done.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage purifying himself in the bathhouse.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba
people.about: The Sage who asks Rabbi Zeira why he needs water poured on him.

terms.meaning: A smaller amount of water (a kav is a measure of volume) that, poured over a man, purifies him after a seminal emission.
The amount of water a ritual bath must hold for immersion.

berakhot-22b-10-10.note: Three Sages, Rav Pappa, Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua and Rava bar Shmuel, ate bread together, and each claimed the honor of leading Grace after Meals. Rav Pappa said he should lead because he had poured nine kav of water over himself. Rava bar Shmuel answered that nine kav suffices only for oneself, while one who acts for others needs forty se'a, and he had immersed in forty se'a. Rav Huna said he should lead, since he had needed neither, having remained pure.
berakhot-22b-10-10.why: The discussion turns on how much water restores purity: nine kav poured over a person or forty se'a, and whether the vessel matters. The meal plays out those levels, and the Gemara then rules against distinguishing purity for oneself from purity for others.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Claims to lead Grace because nine kav of water fell on him.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Claims to lead because he needed no purification at all.

people.name: Rava bar Shmuel
people.about: Claims to lead because he immersed in forty se'a.

terms.meaning: The blessings said after eating bread; one person can lead and recite them on behalf of the whole group.
Measures of volume. Nine kav is a modest amount of water poured over the body; forty se'a is the volume of a ritual bath (mikveh) for full immersion.

berakhot-23a-13-13.note: A student going into a bathroom left his phylacteries in a hole in the wall facing the public street. A prostitute passing by took them, came to the study hall and said: See what so-and-so gave me as my payment. When the student heard this, he went up to the roof, fell and died. At that time the Sages instituted that a person should hold his phylacteries in his hand, covered with his garment, when he goes in.
berakhot-23a-13-13.why: A teaching had just warned against leaving phylacteries in holes facing the public domain, lest passersby take them and the owner fall under suspicion; this incident is the reason behind that warning and the rule that replaced it.

people.name: a student
people.about: Left his phylacteries in a wall hole facing the street; was falsely shamed and died.

people.name: a prostitute
people.about: Took the phylacteries and displayed them in the study hall as payment.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: small leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on the arm and head; they may not be brought into a bathroom carelessly.
The house of study where the Sages and their students learned Torah.

berakhot-23a-20-20.note: Rabba bar bar Ḥana recalled walking behind his teacher Rabbi Yoḥanan: when Rabbi Yoḥanan went into a bathroom holding a book of aggada, he would hand it to his students, but phylacteries he kept, saying: Since the Sages permitted holding them, they will protect me. Rava told the same of Rabbi Naḥman: the book he handed over, the phylacteries he kept, with the same words.
berakhot-23a-20-20.why: The Gemara has been setting out how phylacteries are carried when not worn, rolled in the hand by day or in a pouch by night. These reports show two Sages choosing to keep them in hand, as permitted, rather than give them to someone else.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: Reports what he saw while walking after Rabbi Yoḥanan.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Gave his students his book of aggada but kept his phylacteries.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Reports the same conduct of Rabbi Naḥman.

people.name: Rabbi Naḥman
people.about: Kept his phylacteries in hand, saying they would protect him.

terms.meaning: The non-legal teachings of the Sages: stories, sayings and interpretations of Scripture.
Tefillin: leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on arm and head during prayer and study.

berakhot-24a-3-3.note: Rav Hamnuna, son of Rav Yosef, recalled standing before Rava, who told him to go and bring his phylacteries. He found them in Rava's bed, between the mattress and the pillow, not directly under where his head lay. Rav Hamnuna knew it was the day of Rava's wife's immersion, and understood that Rava had sent him for them to teach the practical law.
berakhot-24a-3-3.why: Rabbi Yirmeya had just ruled that phylacteries kept under one's head at night belong between the pillow and the mattress, off to the side of the head; this incident shows Rava following that ruling in practice.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna, son of Rav Yosef
people.about: Was sent by Rava to fetch his phylacteries and tells what he found.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Kept his phylacteries in his bed and sent his student for them to teach the law.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on arm and head.
The day a wife immerses in a ritual bath after menstruation, after which marital relations are permitted again.

berakhot-24b-7-9.note: Rabbi Abba wanted to move to the Land of Israel and was avoiding his teacher Rav Yehuda, who held that anyone who leaves Babylonia for the Land of Israel transgresses a commandment, citing Jeremiah. Before leaving, he decided to go hear one more teaching at the Sages' assembly. There he heard a teaching on a man who passes wind while praying: he steps back four cubits, waits for the odor to pass, says a short prayer confessing that God made us full of openings, and resumes where he stopped. Rabbi Abba said: Had I come only to hear this, it would have been enough.
berakhot-24b-7-9.why: The Gemara has just distinguished sneezing from above, a good sign in prayer, from sneezing from below, passing wind; this story brings the teaching on what one does after passing wind in the middle of prayer.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Student of Rav Yehuda who wanted to move to the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rabbi Abba's teacher, who held that leaving Babylonia for the Land of Israel is a transgression.

terms.meaning: Here, a man whose job was to recite memorized teachings aloud before the Sages.
The Land of Israel.
About two meters; a standard distance in Jewish law.

berakhot-25b-23-23.note: Rav Aḥai arranged for his son to marry into the family of Rav Yitzḥak bar Shmuel bar Marta. He brought his son into the wedding canopy, but the son could not consummate the marriage. Rav Aḥai went in after him to look into it and saw a Torah scroll lying there. He said to them: Had I not come now, you would have endangered my son's life. He cited a teaching that relations are forbidden in a room with a Torah scroll or phylacteries unless they are taken out or put in a vessel inside a second vessel.
berakhot-25b-23-23.why: The Gemara is discussing what must screen or separate holy objects and bodily matters; this story introduces the rule about a Torah scroll in a bedroom, which Abaye, Rava and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi go on to refine.

people.name: Rav Aḥai
people.about: Father of the groom; found the Torah scroll in the bridal room.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak bar Shmuel bar Marta
people.about: The family his son married into.

terms.meaning: The huppah, here the chamber where the couple first came together.
A double covering, such as a box within a box, which counts as removing a holy object from the room.
Tefillin: leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on arm and head.

berakhot-26a-0-0.note: Mar Zutra visited Rav Ashi's house and saw a Torah scroll in the bedroom of Rav Ashi's son, Mar bar Rav Ashi, with a partition ten handbreadths high set up around it. He asked whose opinion they were following. If Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's, he said, that applies only to someone who has no other room; the Master has another room. Rav Ashi's answer was: It did not occur to me.
berakhot-26a-0-0.why: The Gemara is listing ways to screen a Torah scroll in a room used for marital relations, including Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ten-handbreadth partition; the story limits that partition to someone with no other room.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: Visitor who questioned the partition.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Host; admitted the other room had not occurred to him.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: Rav Ashi's son, in whose bedroom the Torah scroll stood.

terms.meaning: A measure of about 8 to 10 centimeters; ten handbreadths is the standard height of a partition that counts as a separate space.

berakhot-27a-14-14.note: Rav visited the house of Geniva and recited the Shabbat evening prayer on Friday while it was still day. Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba was praying behind him. Rav finished his prayer but did not step back, so as not to interrupt Rabbi Yirmeya's prayer. The Gemara draws three rulings from this: one may pray the Shabbat prayer before Shabbat begins, a student may pray behind his teacher, and one may not pass in front of people who are praying.
berakhot-27a-14-14.why: The Gemara is asking whether the afternoon prayer ends at midafternoon, as Rabbi Yehuda holds, and has just pointed to Rav praying the Shabbat prayer early; it then questions how Rabbi Yirmeya could pray behind his teacher at all.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Prayed the Shabbat prayer early at Geniva's house.

people.name: Geniva
people.about: The Sage whose house Rav visited.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: Was praying behind Rav.

terms.meaning: Friday before nightfall, when Shabbat begins.
At the end of the Amida prayer one takes three steps back; doing so here would have meant passing in front of Rabbi Yirmeya.

berakhot-27b-6-7.note: Avidan reported that once the sky became so overcast that the people thought night had fallen. They went into the synagogue and recited the evening prayer for the end of Shabbat while it was still Shabbat. Then the clouds cleared and the sun shone. They came and asked Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi what to do, and he said: Since they have prayed, they have prayed.
berakhot-27b-6-7.why: The Gemara asked whether a prayer said by mistake can be undone; Avidan's report suggests it cannot, and the Gemara answers that a community is different, since it is not burdened with praying again.

people.name: Avidan
people.about: Reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who ruled that the prayer stood.

terms.term: prayer of the conclusion of Shabbat
terms.meaning: The evening prayer said as Shabbat ends, which marks the passage from Shabbat to the weekday.

berakhot-27b-14-21.note: A student asked Rabbi Yehoshua whether the evening prayer is optional or obligatory; he said optional. Rabban Gamliel said obligatory, raised the question before the assembled Sages, made Rabbi Yehoshua stand to admit his view, and left him standing while he lectured. The angry assembly removed Rabban Gamliel and appointed the eighteen-year-old Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, whose hair miraculously turned white. That day the study hall was opened to all students, and Rabbi Yehoshua's view prevailed over Rabban Gamliel's on an Ammonite convert. Rabban Gamliel went to apologize, found Rabbi Yehoshua's walls black from smithing, was rebuked, and was forgiven for his father's sake. Rabbi Yehoshua then urged his return, and Rabbi Akiva agreed to go to Rabban Gamliel's door the next morning.
berakhot-27b-14-21.why: The mishna says the evening prayer is not fixed, which the Gemara reads as the view that it is optional, the dispute between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua. This is how that dispute unfolded.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Ruled the evening prayer optional; was humiliated by Rabban Gamliel and later forgave him.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Head of the Sages (the Nasi); ruled the prayer obligatory and was removed from office.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Chosen to replace Rabban Gamliel; wise, rich and descended from Ezra.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Considered for the post; later had the gates locked, then agreed to go to Rabban Gamliel.

people.name: Yehuda, the Ammonite convert
people.about: Asked whether he could marry into the Jewish people.

terms.meaning: The head of the Sages and the leader of the Jewish community.
The Gemara's name for the Torah scholars who do battle in the study of Torah.
The man who repeated the lecturer's words aloud to the assembly; when he stopped, the lecture stopped.
Marry a Jewish woman; the Torah bars Ammonites from doing so.

berakhot-28b-5-6.note: When Rabbi Eliezer fell ill, his students came to visit him and asked him to teach them paths of life by which they would earn the World-to-Come. He told them: Be careful of your colleagues' honor; keep your children from logic; seat them, while young, at the knees of Torah scholars; and when you pray, know before Whom you stand. For this, he said, you will earn the World-to-Come.
berakhot-28b-5-6.why: It follows Rabbi Neḥunya ben Hakana's prayers on entering and leaving the study hall, opening a run of related deathbed teachings; its last instruction, to know before Whom one stands in prayer, bears on the chapter's subject of prayer.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Sage who, when ill, gave his students guidance for life.

terms.meaning: The life after this one, in which the righteous are rewarded.
The translation explains this as keeping them from reasoning about verses in ways that lead to heresy.

berakhot-28b-7-10.note: When Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai fell ill, his students visited him, and he began to cry. They asked why. He said that before a human king, whose anger, prison and killing are not forever and who can be appeased or bribed, he would still cry; now he was being led before the King of Kings, whose anger, prison and killing are forever, with two paths before him, to the Garden of Eden or to Gehenna, not knowing which. Asked to bless them, he wished that their fear of Heaven be like their fear of people, since a sinner says: I hope no one sees me. As he died he told them to clear out the vessels because of impurity, and to prepare a chair for Hezekiah, King of Judea, who was coming.
berakhot-28b-7-10.why: The Gemara sets it beside the account of the students visiting Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai's student, on his sickbed, so the teacher's parting words follow the student's.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's teacher; wept on his sickbed in fear of divine judgment.

people.name: Hezekiah, the King of Judea
people.about: The biblical king whom Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai said was coming as he died.

terms.meaning: The place of punishment after death; the Garden of Eden is the place of reward.

terms.term: remove the vessels due to impurity
terms.meaning: A dead body makes everything under the same roof ritually impure, so household items were taken out beforehand.

berakhot-28b-22-23.note: Shimon HaPakuli arranged the eighteen blessings in order before Rabban Gamliel in Yavne. Rabban Gamliel asked the Sages whether anyone knew how to compose the blessing against the heretics, and Shmuel HaKatan stood up and composed it. The next year, leading the prayer, he forgot it and spent two or three hours trying to recall it, and they did not remove him.
berakhot-28b-22-23.why: The Gemara has just asked why the prayer of eighteen blessings has nineteen, answering that the blessing of the heretics was added in Yavne; afterward it asks why Shmuel HaKatan was not removed, since a leader who errs in that blessing is suspected of heresy.

people.name: Shimon HaPakuli
people.about: The Sage who set the eighteen blessings in order

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Nasi, head of the Sages in Yavne, who asks for the new blessing

people.name: Shmuel HaKatan
people.about: The Sage who composes the blessing against the heretics and later forgets it

terms.meaning: The central prayer of the Jewish service, recited standing, also called the Amida.
A blessing added to the prayer asking God to defeat informers and heretics.
The town where the Sages gathered and led the community after the destruction of the Temple.
The person who recites the prayer aloud on behalf of the congregation.

berakhot-29a-5-5.note: The Gemara cites a mishna: Do not be sure of yourself until the day you die, for Yoḥanan the High Priest served in the High Priesthood for eighty years and in the end became a Sadducee.
berakhot-29a-5-5.why: Abaye had said that one who is righteous from the start never turns wicked, to explain why Shmuel HaKatan was not suspected of heresy; the Gemara cites Yoḥanan the High Priest to challenge him.

people.name: Yoḥanan the High Priest
people.about: Served as High Priest for eighty years and finally became a Sadducee.

terms.meaning: A member of a Second Temple group that rejected the Sages' teachings.
The chief priest who served in the Temple in Jerusalem.

berakhot-30a-2-2.note: Rav Ḥisda and Rav Sheshet were walking along the road when Rav Ḥisda stopped, stood and recited the traveler's prayer. Rav Sheshet, who could not see, asked his servant what Rav Ḥisda was doing, and was told he was standing and praying. Rav Sheshet said: Stand me up too, and I will pray. From being good, do not be called wicked.
berakhot-30a-2-2.why: Rav Ḥisda had ruled that the traveler's prayer is said standing, and Rav Sheshet that it may be said walking; here Rav Sheshet stands anyway, showing that his ruling permitted walking but did not prefer it.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Stopped on the road to say the traveler's prayer standing.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: Blind Sage who asked his servant to stand him up to pray as well.

terms.meaning: A short prayer for a safe journey, said when setting out on the road.

berakhot-30b-20-21.note: Abaye was sitting before his teacher Rabba, and Rabba saw that he was very merry. Rabba said: It is written, Rejoice with trembling. Abaye answered: I am wearing phylacteries.
berakhot-30b-20-21.why: Rabba had just taught that the verse rejoice with trembling means that even in rejoicing there should be trembling; here he applies it to his student, who answers that his phylacteries keep him in awe.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rabba's student, rebuked for being too merry.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Abaye's teacher, who quoted the verse to him.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on arm and head; the translation explains that wearing them keeps the fear of God on a person.

berakhot-30b-22-23.note: Rabbi Yirmeya was sitting before Rabbi Zeira, who saw that he was very merry. Rabbi Zeira said to him: It is written, In all sorrow there is profit. Rabbi Yirmeya answered: I am wearing phylacteries.
berakhot-30b-22-23.why: It is the second of a run of stories about holding excessive joy in check, after Rabba's rebuke of Abaye with the verse rejoice with trembling; the reply is the same.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Was very merry and answered that he was wearing phylacteries.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Rebuked Rabbi Yirmeya with a verse from Proverbs.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on arm and head during prayer and study.

berakhot-30b-24-24.note: Mar, son of Ravina, held a wedding feast for his son and saw that the Sages there were getting too merry. He brought out a precious cup worth four hundred zuz and smashed it in front of them, and they grew sad.
berakhot-30b-24-24.why: The Gemara is discussing whether excessive joy is proper; it has just told of Sages rebuked for being too joyful, and follows this with Rav Ashi breaking a glass at his own son's wedding and a mournful song sung at Mar's feast.

people.name: Mar, son of Ravina
people.about: A Babylonian Sage who sobered his son's wedding guests by breaking an expensive cup.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; four hundred zuz was a very large sum.

berakhot-31a-1-1.note: Rav Ashi made a wedding feast for his son and saw that the Sages were very merry. He brought a cup of white glass, broke it in front of them, and they became sad.
berakhot-31a-1-1.why: It follows Mar son of Ravina breaking a cup worth four hundred zuz at his son's wedding, in a run of stories showing that even in rejoicing there should be trembling.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Broke a white glass cup at his son's wedding to sober the guests.

berakhot-31a-2-2.note: At the wedding feast of Mar son of Ravina, the Sages asked Rav Hamnuna Zuti to sing for them. He sang: Woe to us, for we shall die; woe to us, for we shall die. They asked what refrain they should answer, and he told them: Where is Torah and where is mitzva, that protect us?
berakhot-31a-2-2.why: It belongs to a run of wedding stories about curbing excessive joy, and is followed by Rabbi Yoḥanan's teaching in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai that one may not fill one's mouth with laughter in this world.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna Zuti
people.about: Asked to sing at a wedding; sang of death instead.

people.name: Mar son of Ravina
people.about: Host of the wedding feast.

terms.meaning: A commandment, or a good deed done in fulfillment of one.

berakhot-31a-13-14.note: Rav Kahana accompanied Rav Shimi bar Ashi from Pum Nahara to the palm grove of Babylonia. When they arrived, Rav Kahana asked what people mean when they say these palms have been there since Adam. Rav Shimi bar Ashi said he had been reminded of a teaching of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina on Jeremiah's land where no man passed and no person settled: every land Adam decreed would be settled was settled, and every land he decreed would not be settled was not.
berakhot-31a-13-14.why: A teaching had just said one should part from another with a matter of Torah, so that he will remember him; this parting, which ends in a new teaching, is given as an example.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Accompanied Rav Shimi bar Ashi and asked about the palms.

people.name: Rav Shimi bar Ashi
people.about: Answered with a teaching of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina.

terms.meaning: The first human, Adam; the Hebrew word for person in the verse is also adam.

berakhot-32b-29-30.note: A pious man was praying by the road when an officer greeted him. He did not answer, and the officer waited until he finished, then called him a good-for-nothing: his own Torah tells him to guard his life, and the officer could have cut off his head with a sword and no one would have held him to account. The pious man asked what would happen to someone who stopped to return a friend's greeting while standing before a human king; the officer said they would cut off his head. The pious man answered that he had been standing before the King of kings, who lives forever, so all the more so he could not stop. The officer was appeased, and the pious man went home in peace.
berakhot-32b-29-30.why: The discussion is about whether one may break off prayer to answer a ruler's greeting; Rav Yosef has just said one must interrupt for a gentile king because of the danger. This pious man refused to interrupt for a gentile officer and came through unharmed.

people.name: the pious man
people.about: A man praying by the road who will not stop his prayer to return an officer's greeting

people.name: the officer
people.about: A gentile official who greets the praying man and is angered when he gets no reply

terms.meaning: An argument from a lesser case to a greater one: if something holds for a mortal king, it holds all the more for God.

terms.term: the Holy One, Blessed be He
terms.meaning: A common Talmudic name for God.

berakhot-33a-7-9.note: A creature called an arvad was harming people in one place, and they came to tell Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa. He asked to be shown its hole and put his heel over the opening; the arvad came out, bit him, and died. He carried it on his shoulder to the study hall and told those there: it is not the arvad that kills, it is sin that kills. At that moment the Sages said: woe to the man an arvad attacks, and woe to the arvad that Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa attacks.
berakhot-33a-7-9.why: The discussion is about which dangers justify stopping in the middle of prayer, building on the mishna's rule that one does not stop even if a snake is wrapped around one's heel. This story shows a righteous man whom even a deadly creature could not harm.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A Sage the people turn to for help against the creature; it bites him and dies

terms.meaning: A dangerous biting creature, some kind of venomous reptile; the translation leaves the word untranslated.
The house of study where the Sages and their students gathered to learn Torah.

berakhot-33b-18-18.note: A man leading the prayers in front of Rabba added the line: You have shown mercy to the bird's nest, now have mercy and pity on us. Rabba praised him: how well this scholar knows how to appease his Master. Abaye objected that the mishna says such a prayer leader is silenced.
berakhot-33b-18-18.why: The mishna says a prayer leader who invokes God's mercy to the bird's nest is silenced, and two Sages have just argued over why. The Gemara then explains that Rabba agreed with the mishna and only praised the man to sharpen Abaye's mind.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage in whose presence the man leads prayer; he praises the added line

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Objects to Rabba that the mishna says such a leader is silenced

terms.meaning: Served as the leader of communal prayer, who stood before the cabinet holding the Torah scrolls.
The Torah's command to send away the mother bird before taking her eggs or chicks, read here as a sign of God's mercy.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses and explains.

berakhot-33b-20-21.note: A man leading the prayers in front of Rabbi Hanina piled on praises of God: great, mighty, awesome, powerful, strong, fearless, steadfast, honored and more. Rabbi Hanina waited until he finished and then asked whether he had now completed all his Master's praises. Even the three words we do say, great, mighty and awesome, we could not say had Moses not written them in the Torah and the Men of the Great Assembly not put them into the prayer. It is like praising a king who owns thousands of gold coins for having silver ones: an insult, not an honor.
berakhot-33b-20-21.why: The mishna has listed innovations in prayer that get a prayer leader silenced. This story follows as another case of a prayer leader corrected for adding to the set wording of the Sages.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage who rebukes a prayer leader for adding a long string of praises of God

people.name: Moses
people.about: Cited by Rabbi Hanina as the one who first said the words great, mighty and awesome in the Torah

terms.meaning: Served as the leader of communal prayer, who stood before the cabinet holding the Torah scrolls.
An early council of Sages credited with fixing the wording of the prayers.
The central standing prayer of Jewish worship, recited several times a day.

berakhot-34a-10-10.note: A student led the prayers in front of Rabbi Eliezer and dragged the prayer on far too long. Rabbi Eliezer's students complained: how long-winded he is! Rabbi Eliezer answered: is he going on any longer than Moses, who prayed forty days and forty nights?
berakhot-34a-10-10.why: The Gemara has been discussing the structure of the Amida prayer and where personal requests belong. This story, paired with the next one about a very short prayer, shows Rabbi Eliezer allowing a prayer to be as long as the one praying needs.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage who defends a student whose prayer runs very long

people.name: Moses
people.about: Cited by Rabbi Eliezer for praying forty days and forty nights

terms.meaning: Served as the leader of communal prayer, who stood before the cabinet holding the Torah scrolls.

berakhot-34a-11-11.note: Another time a student led the prayers in front of Rabbi Eliezer and cut the prayer far too short. Rabbi Eliezer's students protested: how brief he is! Rabbi Eliezer answered: is he any briefer than Moses, who prayed for his sister Miriam with only the words: Please, God, heal her, please?
berakhot-34a-11-11.why: It pairs with the story just before it, where Rabbi Eliezer defended a very long prayer; together they show he accepted both. The Gemara then learns from Moses' short prayer that one praying for someone else need not mention the person's name.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage who defends a student whose prayer is very short

people.name: Moses
people.about: Cited by Rabbi Eliezer for his five-word prayer to heal Miriam

people.name: Miriam
people.about: Moses' sister, for whose healing he prayed

terms.meaning: Served as the leader of communal prayer, who stood before the cabinet holding the Torah scrolls.

berakhot-34b-26-26.note: Rabban Gamliel's son fell ill, and he sent two scholars to ask Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa to pray for him. Rabbi Hanina went up to his attic, prayed, came down and told them to go, because the fever had left the boy. Asked if he was a prophet, he said no, but he had a tradition: if his prayer flows fluently from his mouth, he knows it was accepted; if not, it was rejected. The scholars wrote down the exact moment. When they came back, Rabban Gamliel swore by the Temple service that they had it exactly: at that very hour the fever broke and the boy asked for water.
berakhot-34b-26-26.why: The mishna mentions Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa and his sign that a fluent prayer is an accepted one; the Gemara follows with stories of how his prayers worked.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Father of the sick boy; he sends scholars to ask Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa to pray

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A Sage whose prayer heals the boy; he knows it was accepted by how fluently it came

terms.meaning: An oath formula: Rabban Gamliel swears by the worship once performed in the Temple in Jerusalem.

berakhot-34b-27-27.note: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa went to study Torah with Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai, whose son fell ill. Rabbi Yohanan asked him to pray for the boy so that he would live. Rabbi Hanina put his head between his knees, prayed, and the boy lived. Rabbi Yohanan said that if he himself had kept his head between his knees all day, Heaven would have paid him no attention. His wife asked: is Hanina greater than you? He said no, but Hanina is like a servant before the King, and he is like a minister before the King.
berakhot-34b-27-27.why: The mishna mentions Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa's power in prayer; this is the second of the Gemara's stories showing it, after the healing of Rabban Gamliel's son.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A student of Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai whose prayer saves his teacher's son

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: Hanina's teacher; his son falls ill and he asks Hanina to pray

people.name: his wife
people.about: Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai's wife, who asks whether Hanina is greater than he is

berakhot-37a-13-13.note: Rabban Gamliel and the Sages were dining in an upper room in Jericho and were served dates. Rabban Gamliel gave Rabbi Akiva the honor of leading the blessing afterward, and Rabbi Akiva quickly recited a single blessing that sums up the three of the Grace after Meals. Rabban Gamliel said: Akiva, how long will you keep sticking your head into disputes? Rabbi Akiva answered: our teacher, you say one thing and your colleagues say another, but you yourself taught us that when one disagrees with many, the law follows the many.
berakhot-37a-13-13.why: The Gemara has just cited a dispute: for foods of the seven species, Rabban Gamliel requires the full three blessings of Grace after Meals, while the Rabbis say one abridged blessing is enough. Here Rabbi Akiva follows the Rabbis in front of Rabban Gamliel himself.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The leader of the Sages; he hands Rabbi Akiva the honor of the blessing, then rebukes him

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Recites the short blessing and defends it by Rabban Gamliel's own rule

terms.meaning: A short after-blessing that sums up in one paragraph the three main blessings of the full Grace after Meals.
The blessings said after eating a meal with bread.

berakhot-38a-15-15.note: The Sages kept praising the son of Rav Zevid to Rabbi Zeira as a great man and an expert in blessings, and Rabbi Zeira asked them to bring him when he came. When he visited and was served bread, he said the blessing with the word motzi rather than hamotzi. Rabbi Zeira was annoyed: is this the great expert they talk about? Had he said hamotzi he would have taught something, but saying motzi teaches nothing. The Gemara explains that he chose motzi to keep himself out of the dispute.
berakhot-38a-15-15.why: The Gemara has just set out the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Nehemya over whether the blessing on bread should say hamotzi or motzi. This story shows a scholar choosing the wording that is valid by every opinion.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who wants to meet the praised expert and is let down by his blessing

people.name: son of Rav Zevid
people.about: Brother of Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Zevid, praised by the Sages as an expert in blessings

terms.meaning: Two wordings of the blessing over bread, 'Who brings forth' or 'Who brought forth' bread from the earth; the Sages disputed which tense hamotzi carries, but all agree motzi means the past.
Jewish law; the ruling that is followed in practice.

berakhot-39a-3-4.note: Two students sat before bar Kappara when cooked cabbage, Damascene plums and young birds were served. Bar Kappara let one of them say the blessing, and he rushed to bless the birds first; the other student mocked him. Bar Kappara was angry. First he said he was angry not at the one who blessed but at the one who mocked: if your friend acts like someone who never tasted meat, why mock him? Then he said he was angry at the one who blessed: if there is no wisdom here, is there no elder here to ask? The teaching adds that neither of them lived out the year.
berakhot-39a-3-4.why: The Gemara has been asking which blessing goes on boiled vegetables, and it tries to read the two students' dispute as that same disagreement. It then rejects that reading and says they disagreed over whether the food one prefers or the more nourishing cabbage comes first.

people.name: bar Kappara
people.about: A teacher before whom the students sit; he grows angry at both of them

people.name: two students
people.about: One blesses the birds first, the other mocks him; neither lives out the year

terms.meaning: Young birds, here served cooked as a dish.
An older scholar; bar Kappara means they should have asked him which blessing to say first.

berakhot-41b-3-4.note: Rav Hisda and Rav Hamnuna were at a meal and were served dates and pomegranates. Rav Hamnuna said the blessing on the dates first. Rav Hisda asked: don't you hold the rule that whatever comes first in the verse about the Land of Israel's produce comes first in blessing, and the pomegranate comes before the date? Rav Hamnuna answered that the date is second after the word land, in a land of olive oil and honey, while the pomegranate is fifth after it. Rav Hisda said in admiration: who will give us iron legs so that we can serve you and hear you?
berakhot-41b-3-4.why: The Gemara has been reading the verse praising the Land of Israel for the order of blessings and for legal measures. This story applies its rule about blessing order to an actual meal.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who questions why the dates were blessed before the pomegranates

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Sage who blesses the dates first and explains why by counting from the word land

terms.meaning: In this verse, honey means dates, from which date honey is made, so the dates count as the second item after land.

berakhot-42a-2-3.note: Rav Yehuda was preparing his son's wedding at the house of Rav Yehuda bar Haviva when sweet dessert bread was served. He heard the people saying the blessing over bread, Who brings forth bread from the earth, and asked what that sound was. They said yes, that was their blessing, citing Rabbi Mona, and that Shmuel ruled like him. Rav Yehuda said they had it wrong: Shmuel said the law does not follow Rabbi Mona. They objected that he himself had quoted Shmuel saying the full bread blessing is said over wafers. He answered that the wafers were different, because a person had made his meal on them.
berakhot-42a-2-3.why: The Gemara is asking when sweet bread served as dessert counts as real bread; Rav Nahman has just said it does when it is eaten as a meal. Rav Yehuda's answer draws the same line.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage arranging his son's wedding who corrects the guests' blessing over dessert bread

people.name: Rav Yehuda bar Haviva
people.about: The man at whose house the wedding preparations take place

people.name: Rabbi Mona
people.about: A Sage cited for the view that dessert bread gets the full blessing over bread

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage whose ruling on Rabbi Mona is in dispute between Rav Yehuda and the guests

terms.meaning: Sweetened, spiced baked goods eaten after a meal, like a pastry.
A legal device using shared food that lets people carry in a shared courtyard, or cook on a festival for Shabbat.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the mishna.

berakhot-42a-4-4.note: Rav Pappa visited the home of Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan. After the meal was over, something more to eat was brought in, and Rav Pappa took it and ate without saying a new blessing. His hosts asked whether he did not hold that once a meal is finished one may not eat again without a blessing. He answered that the rule, correctly stated, speaks of the table being 'removed', not of the meal being finished.
berakhot-42a-4-4.why: The Gemara is working out when a meal counts as over, so that further food needs its own blessing; right after, Rava and Rabbi Zeira argue the same question at the Exilarch's house, using Rav Pappa's 'removed' wording.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Babylonian Sage and head of an academy, a visitor here.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan
people.about: A Babylonian Sage, the host of the meal.

terms.meaning: In Talmudic times each diner ate at a small table that was carried away when the meal ended. Taking it away, not just stopping eating, marks the meal's end.

berakhot-42a-5-5.note: Rava and Rabbi Zeira were guests at the house of the Exilarch. After the table had been cleared, a portion of food was sent to them from the Exilarch. Rava ate it and Rabbi Zeira did not. Rabbi Zeira asked him: don't you hold that once the table is cleared one may not eat? Rava answered that they depended on the Exilarch's table.
berakhot-42a-5-5.why: The Gemara is asking when a meal is over, so that eating more needs a new blessing; Rav Pappa has just said it is when the table is cleared. Rava's answer adds that guests' meals are not over while their host's is not.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who eats the food sent after the table was cleared

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who does not eat it and asks Rava why he did

people.name: the Exilarch
people.about: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who hosts the two Sages

terms.meaning: In the Sages' time each diner ate from a small table that was taken away at the end of the meal, so removing it marked the meal's end.

berakhot-42b-12-13.note: When Rav died, his students followed his coffin. On the way back they decided to eat bread by the Dannak River. After eating, they sat and could not settle a question: does the mishna's rule on saying the blessing together apply only when diners recline, or also when they agreed beforehand to eat at a certain place? Rav Adda bar Ahava stood, turned his torn cloak around so the tear was behind him, and tore it again, saying: Rav is dead, and we have not learned the laws of Grace after Meals. Then an elder came, set the mishna against a teaching from the early Sages, and resolved it: since they said let us go and eat in such-and-such a place, it is as if they reclined.
berakhot-42b-12-13.why: The Gemara has just answered a contradiction between the mishna, which says only reclining makes a shared meal, and a teaching that sitting is enough: planning to eat at a named place counts. The story shows Rav's students stuck on that very question.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A great teacher whose death and funeral open the story

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: One of Rav's students, who tears his garment a second time in grief

people.name: an elder
people.about: An older man who resolves the students' question

terms.meaning: Diners in the Sages' time lay on couches for a formal meal; reclining together made it a shared meal with one blessing for all.
Tearing one's clothing is a Jewish sign of mourning.
The blessings said after a meal with bread.

berakhot-43b-9-9.note: Rav Pappa visited the house of Rav Huna son of Rav Ika, and they were served scented oil and a myrtle branch. Rav Pappa said the blessing over the myrtle first and then over the oil. Rav Huna asked whether he did not hold that the law follows Rabban Gamliel's deciding opinion, oil first. Rav Pappa replied that Rava had ruled like Beit Hillel. The Gemara says this was not so; Rav Pappa said it to get himself out of an awkward spot.
berakhot-43b-9-9.why: The Gemara has just cited a dispute over whether oil or myrtle is blessed first, with Rabban Gamliel deciding for oil and Rabbi Yohanan ruling that the law follows him. This story shows a Sage who acted against that ruling and how he excused himself.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A guest who blesses the myrtle before the oil

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Ika
people.about: The host, who questions Rav Pappa's order of blessings

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage whom Rav Pappa claims ruled like Beit Hillel; the Gemara says he did not

terms.meaning: A fragrant plant; Jews say a blessing over pleasant smells, such as myrtle or scented oil.
The school of the Sage Hillel, which here says the myrtle is blessed before the oil.
Rabban Gamliel, who settled the dispute between the schools of Hillel and Shammai in favor of oil first.

berakhot-44a-2-3.note: Rabba bar bar Hana recalled going with Rabbi Yohanan to eat the fruit of Genosar. When a hundred of them went, each brought him ten fruits; when ten went, each brought a hundred, and every hundred filled a basket of three se'a. Rabbi Yohanan ate them all and would swear he had not had a proper meal. Rabbi Abbahu ate until a fly would slip off his forehead; Rav Ami and Rav Asi ate until their hair fell out; Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish ate until he became confused, and Rabbi Yohanan would tell the household of the Nasi, and Rabbi Yehuda Nesia would send officers to bring him home.
berakhot-44a-2-3.why: The mishna has said that salted food can be the main dish with bread secondary, and Rav Ashi explained that this was for people eating the very sweet fruit of Genosar. These tales show how sweet and plentiful that fruit was.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: The Sage who tells of going with Rabbi Yohanan to eat Genosar fruit

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Eats huge amounts of the fruit and swears he has not had a meal

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
people.about: Eats the fruit until he becomes confused and has to be taken home

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: Head of the Nasi's household, who sends officers to bring Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish home

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Eats until a fly would slip from his forehead

terms.meaning: A region by the Sea of Galilee famous for its very sweet fruit.
A measure of volume; a basket of three se'a is a large basket.
The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel.

berakhot-44b-14-15.note: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were sitting together when raw vegetables were served before the fourth hour of the day. Ameimar and Rav Ashi ate; Mar Zutra did not. They asked him whether he was following Rabbi Yitzhak's saying that one may not talk to a person who ate vegetables that early because of the smell, since he was talking to them anyway. He answered that he followed Rabbi Yitzhak's other saying: it is forbidden to eat raw vegetables before the fourth hour.
berakhot-44b-14-15.why: The Gemara has just quoted both of Rabbi Yitzhak's sayings about eating vegetables early in the day. This story shows Mar Zutra telling them apart.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage who eats the raw vegetables

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: A Sage who will not eat the raw vegetables and explains which rule he follows

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who eats the raw vegetables

terms.meaning: The fourth hour of the day, counted from daybreak, so roughly mid-morning.
