berakhot-45b-17-18.note: Yehuda bar Mareimar, Mar bar Rav Ashi and Rav Aha of Difti ate bread together. None was greater than the others, so none was the obvious one to lead the blessing. They wondered whether the rule that three who eat together must join in a shared blessing applies only when one of them is a great man, and whether equals do better to bless separately. Each blessed for himself. Then they went to Mareimar, who told them they had fulfilled the blessing but not the zimmun, and that a zimmun cannot be done after the fact.
berakhot-45b-17-18.why: The Gemara has been discussing when diners must or may split up for the blessing after a meal, including a teaching that two learned people who ate together should bless separately. This story asks whether the same holds for three equals, and Mareimar's answer is no.

people.name: Yehuda bar Mareimar
people.about: One of three equal scholars who eat together

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: One of the three

people.name: Rav Aha of Difti
people.about: One of the three

people.name: Mareimar
people.about: The Sage they ask afterward, who says they missed the zimmun

terms.meaning: The invitation to bless together: when three or more eat together, one invites the others to join in Grace after Meals.
The blessings said after a meal with bread.

berakhot-46a-0-1.note: Rabbi Zeira fell ill, and Rabbi Abbahu, visiting him, vowed that if the little man with the scorched legs, his nickname for Rabbi Zeira, recovered, he would make a feast for the Sages. Rabbi Zeira recovered and Rabbi Abbahu made the feast. When it was time to break bread, Rabbi Abbahu asked Rabbi Zeira to do it; Rabbi Zeira reminded him of Rabbi Yohanan's rule that the host breaks bread, and Rabbi Abbahu broke it. When it was time for Grace after Meals, Rabbi Abbahu asked Rabbi Zeira to lead it, and Rabbi Zeira cited Rav Huna of Babylonia: whoever breaks bread leads the blessing. The text does not say here who led it.
berakhot-46a-0-1.why: The Gemara has been discussing who should lead the blessings at a meal. It goes on to explain that Rabbi Abbahu followed the teaching that the host breaks bread and the guest leads Grace, so that the guest can bless the host.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Falls ill and recovers; the guest of honor at the feast

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Vows a feast for the Sages if Rabbi Zeira recovers, and hosts it

terms.meaning: Say the blessing over bread and cut it for everyone at the start of the meal.
The blessings said after a meal with bread.

berakhot-46b-3-3.note: Mar Zutra was visiting Rav Ashi's home when a death struck the household and Rav Ashi was in mourning. Mar Zutra recited one long combined blessing: it opened with "Who is good and does good," went on to praise God as the true Judge who takes away with justice and does in His world as He wills, and closed with a prayer that God, who repairs the breaches in Israel, repair this breach for life.
berakhot-46b-3-3.why: The Gemara has just read a baraita about what is said in a house of mourning and concluded that "Who is good and does good" is said there as well as "the true Judge." Mar Zutra's blessing shows both said together.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: A Sage who happened to visit Rav Ashi's home and recited the blessing.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage in whose home the death occurred.

terms.term: Who is good and does good
terms.meaning: A blessing thanking God for good; it is also the fourth blessing of Grace after Meals.
A blessing said on hearing of a death, accepting God's judgment as just.

berakhot-46b-13-13.note: Rav and Rabbi Hiyya were eating a meal in the presence of Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi). Rabbi told Rav: "Stand, wash your hands." Rabbi Hiyya saw that Rav was trembling, afraid he had done something wrong at the meal. Rabbi Hiyya reassured him: "Son of noblemen, he is telling you to review Grace after Meals," since the first to wash at the end of a meal would be the one to lead the blessing.
berakhot-46b-13-13.why: The Gemara has just cited Rav's rule that whoever washes his hands first at the end of a meal leads Grace after Meals; this meal shows that practice in action.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage dining before Rabbi, told to wash his hands.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage at the same meal who explained Rabbi's instruction to Rav.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the host before whom they ate.

terms.meaning: The set of blessings said after eating a meal with bread.

berakhot-47a-1-1.note: Ravin and Abaye were riding along a road. Ravin's donkey went ahead of Abaye's, and Ravin did not say "Let the Master go first." Abaye said to himself that since Ravin came up from the Land of Israel he had become arrogant. But at the door of the synagogue Ravin said, "Let the Master enter." Abaye asked, "Until now was I not Master?" Ravin answered that Rabbi Yohanan taught one defers to a greater person only at a doorway that has a mezuza.
berakhot-47a-1-1.why: The Sages have just taught that one does not show deference on roads or bridges; this journey illustrates the rule, and the Gemara goes on to refine Rabbi Yohanan's "mezuza" wording.

people.name: Ravin
people.about: A Sage who had come from the Land of Israel; he rode ahead and later deferred at the synagogue door.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage traveling with Ravin who thought him arrogant.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage whose teaching Ravin quoted.

terms.meaning: A small parchment scroll with Torah verses fixed to the doorpost of a home.
A Babylonian way of referring to the Land of Israel.

berakhot-47a-11-11.note: Rav and Shmuel were sitting at a meal when Rav Shimi bar Hiyya arrived late and began eating in a hurry. Rav asked him why he was rushing: to join them for the zimmun? They had already eaten. Shmuel answered Rav that they had not really finished: if someone brought truffles or a young pigeon for Rav, would they not eat it?
berakhot-47a-11-11.why: The discussion turns back to the zimmun; the exchange asks whether a latecomer can join diners who have stopped eating, and Shmuel's answer is that they are still in their meal while they would still eat more.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage at the meal; Shmuel calls him Abba.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage at the meal who argued they had not yet finished.

people.name: Rav Shimi bar Hiyya
people.about: A latecomer who hurried to eat.

terms.meaning: The invitation to say Grace after Meals together, recited when at least three people have eaten as a group; one person leads and the others respond.

berakhot-47b-6-6.note: Rami bar Hama would not include Rav Menashya bar Tahlifa in a zimmun, although Rav Menashya had studied Sifra, Sifrei and halakhot. When Rami bar Hama died, Rava said he died only because he had refused to include Rav Menashya. The Gemara asks why, given the teaching that one who studied but did not serve Torah scholars is an am ha'aretz, and answers that Rav Menashya had served the Sages; Rami bar Hama simply did not check carefully.
berakhot-47b-6-6.why: The Gemara has just listed opinions on who counts as an am ha'aretz, who may not be included in a zimmun, and Rav Huna ruled like the opinion that even one who studied but did not serve scholars is one. This case tests that ruling.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: A Sage who refused to include Rav Menashya bar Tahlifa in a zimmun, and died.

people.name: Rav Menashya bar Tahlifa
people.about: A scholar of Sifra, Sifrei and halakhot who, the Gemara says, had served the Sages.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who said Rami bar Hama died because of this.

terms.meaning: The invitation to say Grace after Meals together, recited when at least three people have eaten as a group; one person leads and the others respond.
Literally "people of the land": someone not careful in religious law or learning; the Sages debate the exact definition.
Early collections of the Sages' interpretations of the books of Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy.

berakhot-48a-2-2.note: When Abaye and Rava were children they sat before Rabba, who asked them, "To whom does one recite blessings?" They answered, "To the All-Merciful." He asked, "And where does the All-Merciful reside?" Rava pointed to the ceiling; Abaye went outside and pointed toward the sky. Rabba told them, "You will both become Sages," quoting the saying that a cucumber can be recognized from its blossom.
berakhot-48a-2-2.why: The Gemara has just ruled, following Rav Nahman, that a minor who knows to Whom one blesses is included in a zimmun; this scene shows children being tested on exactly that.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: As a child, he went outside and pointed to the sky.

people.name: Rava
people.about: As a child, he pointed to the ceiling.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The teacher who questioned the two boys.

terms.meaning: A common Aramaic name for God.

berakhot-48a-4-5.note: King Yannai and his queen were eating together, but since Yannai had killed the Sages there was no one to lead Grace after Meals. The queen made him swear not to harm the man she brought, then brought her brother Shimon ben Shatah and seated him between them. Yannai boasted of the honor he gave him; Shimon replied that the Torah honors him, not the king, and Yannai complained that he does not accept authority. Given a cup to bless over, Shimon asked how he could say "from Whom Yannai and his companions have eaten" when he had eaten nothing. He drank that cup, was given another, and recited the blessing.
berakhot-48a-4-5.why: The Gemara has been asking how much and what kind of food one must eat to join a zimmun; right after, Rabbi Yohanan says Shimon ben Shatah acted on his own, since one cannot lead others in Grace without eating an olive's bulk of grain.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: The king who had killed the Sages and needed someone to lead Grace after Meals.

people.name: the queen
people.about: Yannai's wife and Shimon ben Shatah's sister, who brought him under oath.

people.name: Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: The queen's brother, a Sage, who led the blessing.

terms.meaning: The set of blessings said after eating a meal with bread.
A cup of wine held by the leader while reciting Grace after Meals.

berakhot-49a-14-14.note: Rabbi Zeira invited Rav Hisda to come and teach. Rav Hisda refused: he had not yet learned Grace after Meals, so how could he teach? He explained that at the Exilarch's house he had led Grace, and Rav Sheshet stiffened his neck at him like a snake because he left out covenant, Torah and sovereignty. He had followed Rav's view that omitting them is acceptable, since covenant does not apply to women, and Torah and sovereignty apply neither to women nor slaves. Rabbi Zeira answered: you abandoned all those other Sages and followed Rav?
berakhot-49a-14-14.why: The Gemara is working out what each blessing of Grace after Meals must contain and how it ends; this exchange shows that leaving covenant, Torah and sovereignty out of the second blessing drew a sharp rebuke.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: The Sage who invited Rav Hisda to teach and criticized his choice.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The Sage who led Grace at the Exilarch's house and was rebuked.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: The Sage who angrily challenged Rav Hisda's blessing.

terms.meaning: The official head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.
Themes traditionally mentioned in Grace: the covenant of circumcision, the gift of the Torah, and the kingdom of David.

berakhot-49a-21-21.note: Giddel bar Manyumi was standing before Rav Nahman when Rav Nahman forgot the special Shabbat passage in Grace after Meals and went back to the beginning to say it all again. Giddel asked why he did that. Rav Nahman answered that Rabbi Sheila taught in Rav's name: one who errs goes back to the beginning.
berakhot-49a-21-21.why: Just before, Rav Giddel taught in Rav's name a short blessing for one who forgot Shabbat. Rav Nahman's conduct contradicts that, and the Gemara next resolves it: the short blessing works only before starting "Who is good and does good."

people.name: Giddel bar Manyumi
people.about: He saw Rav Nahman restart Grace and asked why.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who forgot the Shabbat passage and started Grace over.

terms.meaning: The set of blessings said after eating a meal with bread.

berakhot-50a-12-12.note: Ravina and Rav Hama bar Buzi were at a meal at the Exilarch's house. At the end, Rav Hama got up and went around looking to gather a hundred people so the zimmun for a hundred could be said. Ravina told him there was no need, because Rava had ruled like Rabbi Akiva.
berakhot-50a-12-12.why: The Mishna gives two views: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says the zimmun wording grows with the size of the crowd; Rabbi Akiva says it stays the same once there are ten. Rava rules like Rabbi Akiva, and this scene shows that ruling applied.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who told Rav Hama not to bother gathering a hundred.

people.name: Rav Hama bar Buzi
people.about: A Sage who tried to gather a hundred diners.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage whose ruling Ravina quoted.

terms.meaning: The invitation to say Grace after Meals together, recited when at least three people have eaten as a group; one person leads and the others respond.
The official head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

berakhot-50a-15-15.note: Rafram bar Pappa came to the synagogue of Abei Givar and was called to read from the Torah. He said "Bless the Lord" and stopped, without adding "the blessed One." The whole congregation cried out "Bless the Lord the blessed One." Rava said to him: "You black pot, why get involved in a dispute? Besides, the common practice follows Rabbi Yishmael."
berakhot-50a-15-15.why: The Mishna records Rabbi Akiva's call "Bless the Lord" against Rabbi Yishmael's "Bless the Lord the blessed One." Rava has ruled like Rabbi Akiva for the zimmun, yet here he says synagogue practice follows Rabbi Yishmael.

people.name: Rafram bar Pappa
people.about: A Sage who used the shorter call to bless before reading the Torah.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who told him practice follows Rabbi Yishmael.

terms.meaning: An affectionate nickname for a Torah scholar who works hard at study.
The call to the congregation before reading the Torah; the congregation answers with a blessing.

berakhot-50b-9-9.note: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were eating together when dates and pomegranates were brought. Mar Zutra tossed some fruit to Rav Ashi. Rav Ashi asked him whether he did not hold that one may not throw food. Mar Zutra said that rule was about bread. Rav Ashi quoted a teaching that, like bread, other foods may not be thrown; Mar Zutra answered with another teaching that bread may not be thrown but other foods may.
berakhot-50b-9-9.why: The Sages have just listed ways to show respect for bread, including not throwing it. This meal asks whether the rule covers other food, and the Gemara reconciles the two teachings: food that gets spoiled by throwing may not be thrown.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage eating with Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: He tossed fruit to Rav Ashi and defended it.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: He objected that food may not be thrown.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages of the Mishna's era that was not included in the Mishna itself.

berakhot-51b-5-6.note: Ulla visited Rav Naḥman, ate, led Grace after Meals, and handed the cup of blessing to Rav Naḥman. Rav Naḥman asked him to send the cup to his wife Yalta. Ulla refused, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan that a woman's offspring are blessed only through her husband, from the verse: He will bless the fruit of your body. Yalta heard, rose in a rage, went into the wine store and broke four hundred barrels of wine. At Rav Naḥman's request Ulla sent her another cup with word that all the wine in the barrel was wine of blessing. She sent back: from peddlers, words, and from rags, lice.
berakhot-51b-5-6.why: The Gemara has just listed how the cup of blessing is handled, ending with sending it to one's household so one's wife will be blessed; Ulla's refusal disputes that last practice.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A visiting Sage who leads Grace after Meals and refuses to send Yalta the cup

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Ulla's host, Yalta's husband

people.name: Yalta
people.about: Rav Naḥman's wife, who smashes the wine barrels in anger

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage whose teaching Ulla quotes

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: A Sage who taught the same idea in a baraita

terms.meaning: The blessings said after eating bread, sometimes over a cup of wine.
The cup of wine held while leading Grace after Meals, then drunk and shared.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

berakhot-53b-16-16.note: Two students ate and did not say Grace. One forgot by accident, and following Beit Shammai he went back to where he had eaten, and found a purse of gold. The other skipped it on purpose and, following Beit Hillel, did not go back, and a lion ate him.
berakhot-53b-16-16.why: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree over whether one who forgot Grace must return to where he ate, and the Gemara has just said that even Beit Hillel require a return when it was skipped on purpose. The two students show the results.

terms.meaning: The schools of two early Sages, Shammai and Hillel, who often disagreed on Jewish law.
The set of blessings said after eating a meal with bread.

berakhot-53b-17-17.note: Rabba bar bar Hana was traveling with a caravan when he ate and forgot to say Grace. He thought: if I tell them I forgot to bless, they will tell me to bless here, since God can be blessed anywhere. Better to say I forgot a golden dove. He told them to wait for him because he had forgotten a golden dove, went back, said the blessing, and found a golden dove.
berakhot-53b-17-17.why: The discussion is about whether one who forgot Grace must go back to where he ate, as Beit Shammai hold; this journey follows the two students who went back, or did not, with their rewards.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage traveling with a caravan who went back to say Grace.

terms.meaning: The set of blessings said after eating a meal with bread.

berakhot-54a-10-10.note: A man was walking along the right side of the Euphrates when a lion attacked him. A miracle happened and he was saved. He came to Rava, who told him: every time you reach that place, say the blessing "Blessed... Who performed a miracle for me in this place."
berakhot-54a-10-10.why: Rabbi Yohanan has derived from Jethro's words that one blesses God for a miracle. The Gemara asks whether that applies only to a miracle for the many, and brings this case to show an individual blesses too.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who told the rescued man which blessing to say.

berakhot-54a-12-12.note: Mar, son of Ravina, was walking in the marketplace of Mehoza when a wild camel attacked him. The wall split open, he went inside it, and was saved. After that, at the willows (where a spring had once appeared for him when he was thirsty) he would bless God "Who performed a miracle for me in the willows and with the camel," and at the Mehoza market, "with the camel and in the willows."
berakhot-54a-12-12.why: The Gemara asked whether one blesses for a miracle done for an individual; these cases show one does, and the Sages conclude that everyone blesses for a public miracle, but only the person himself for a private one.

people.name: Mar, son of Ravina
people.about: A Sage saved from a wild camel, who blessed God for it.

berakhot-55a-5-5.note: A noblewoman told Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi El'ai that his face looked like those of pig farmers and moneylenders, people who live well without hard work. He told her that both trades were forbidden to him. Rather, between his lodging and the study hall there were twenty-four bathrooms, and on his way he stopped to relieve himself in every one of them.
berakhot-55a-5-5.why: Rav Yehuda had praised lingering in the bathroom, and the Gemara has just distinguished healthy lingering from harmful straining. This anecdote shows the benefit.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi El'ai
people.about: A Sage whose healthy face a noblewoman commented on.

people.name: a matron
people.about: A noblewoman who remarked on his well-fed face.

terms.meaning: Moneylenders who charge interest, which the Torah forbids among Jews.

berakhot-55b-15-15.note: Rabbi Bena'a, passed down through a long chain of Sages, recalled that there were twenty-four dream interpreters in Jerusalem. He once had a dream and went to all of them. Each gave a different interpretation, and every one of them came true for him.
berakhot-55b-15-15.why: The discussion is about whether dreams are true or false; this account backs the saying that "all dreams follow the mouth" of the interpreter, which the Gemara then traces to a verse and limits.

people.name: Rabbi Bena'a
people.about: The elder who went to all twenty-four interpreters.

berakhot-56a-0-0.note: The Roman emperor challenged Rabbi Yehoshua son of Rabbi Hananya: you Jews say you are very wise, so tell me what I will see in my dream. Rabbi Yehoshua said he would see the Persians capture him, enslave him, and make him herd unclean animals with a golden staff. The emperor thought about it all day, and that night he dreamed it. Likewise King Shapur of Persia asked Shmuel, who said he would see the Romans take him captive and make him grind date pits in golden mills. He thought about it all day and that night he dreamed it.
berakhot-56a-0-0.why: Rabbi Yonatan has just taught that a person is shown in a dream only the thoughts of his heart; both rulers dream what they spent the day thinking about.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler who challenged Rabbi Yehoshua.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua son of Rabbi Hananya
people.about: The Sage who foretold the emperor's dream.

people.name: King Shapur
people.about: The king of Persia who challenged Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who foretold Shapur's dream.

terms.meaning: Animals the Torah forbids Jews to eat, such as pigs.

berakhot-56a-1-18.note: Bar Haddaya interpreted dreams favorably for those who paid him and unfavorably for those who did not. Abaye and Rava brought him the same dreams; Abaye paid and Rava did not, so Abaye heard of profit and honor, and Rava of loss, his wife's death and arrest, and the next day Rava was seized when the king's treasury was robbed. Alone, Rava was told he would take two blows, and blind men fighting struck him twice. Later he paid and heard good things. When bar Haddaya dropped a book saying all dreams follow the mouth, Rava called him a scoundrel, forgave all but his wife's death, and prayed he be handed to a merciless kingdom. Bar Haddaya fled to Rome, held back a reading from the king's unpaying wardrobe keeper, and was tied between two cedars and split in two.
berakhot-56a-1-18.why: The Gemara is collecting teachings on how dreams come true, such as which dreams are fulfilled and that dreams show a person's own thoughts. This story makes the point that a dream's outcome follows the way it is interpreted.

people.name: Bar Haddaya
people.about: An interpreter of dreams whose readings depended on whether he was paid.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Paid bar Haddaya and received favorable readings of his dreams.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Saw the same dreams as Abaye but did not pay at first, and received dire readings.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Father of Rava's wife, whose death bar Haddaya foretold.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; bar Haddaya asks for one as his fee.
Tefillin: small leather boxes holding Torah verses, worn by men during prayer. One of the verses inside mentions a firstborn donkey.
Psalms of praise sung on festivals; the Egyptian hallel celebrates the Exodus from Egypt.
An academy of Torah study, led by a head who teaches the students.

berakhot-56b-3-5.note: A heretic told Rabbi Yishmael one dream after another, and each time Rabbi Yishmael read it as a confession: relations with his mother and his sister, kidnapping and selling an Israelite, adultery, and sending away two wives without a divorce. When Rabbi Yishmael said that peeling eggs meant he stripped the dead, the heretic said every reading was true except that one; just then a woman came and said the cloak he wore belonged to a man who had died and whom he had stripped. Last, he dreamed his father had left him property in Cappadocia. Learning that neither had ever been there, Rabbi Yishmael read the name as Greek for beam and ten, told him to look in the tenth beam, and he found it full of coins.
berakhot-56b-3-5.why: The Gemara has been gathering dream interpretations by Sages, including Rabbi Yishmael's reading of his nephew's dream. After these examples it turns to lists of what particular images in dreams signify.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A Sage who interprets the heretic's dreams.

terms.meaning: Here, a man who rejected the Sages' teachings; the text does not name him.
A woman in the first stage of Jewish marriage, before she lives with her husband; relations with another man count as adultery.
A Jewish marriage ends only with a bill of divorce, called a get; sending a wife away without one leaves her still married.

berakhot-57a-16-16.note: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, each had a dream. Rav Pappa dreamed he entered a marsh and became head of a yeshiva; Rav Huna dreamed he entered a forest and became head of the advanced students. Some say both dreamed of a marsh, but Rav Pappa dreamed a drum hung from his neck and so became head of the yeshiva, while Rav Huna, who had no drum, led only the advanced students. Rav Ashi said that he had dreamed he entered a marsh, hung a drum and beat it.
berakhot-57a-16-16.why: The Gemara has just taught that dreaming of a marsh means one will head a yeshiva and dreaming of a forest means one will head the advanced students. These Sages' dreams are offered as cases where those signs came true.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Dreamed of a marsh and was appointed head of a yeshiva.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Dreamed of a forest and was appointed head of the advanced students.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Reports his own dream of entering a marsh and beating a drum.

terms.meaning: An academy of Torah study, led by a head who teaches the students.
The kalla: a gathering of the most accomplished students, taught by their own leader.

berakhot-58a-9-11.note: Rav Sheshet, who was blind, went along with everyone to greet the king. A heretic mocked him: whole jugs go to the river, but where do broken ones go? Rav Sheshet said he would show he knew more. Two troops passed with rising noise, and each time the heretic said the king was coming and Rav Sheshet said he was not. When a third passed in silence, Rav Sheshet said the king was surely coming now. Asked how he knew, he said earthly royalty is like heavenly royalty: God came to Elijah not in wind, earthquake or fire but in a still small voice. When the king came Rav Sheshet blessed him, and the heretic mocked him for blessing someone he could not see. Some say the heretic's friends gouged out his eyes; others, that Rav Sheshet fixed his gaze on him and he became a pile of bones.
berakhot-58a-9-11.why: The Gemara has just taught the blessing said on seeing a king and Rabbi Yoḥanan's advice to run to see even non-Jewish kings. Rav Sheshet goes and recites the blessing although he is blind.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A blind Sage who goes to greet the king and outwits the heretic.

terms.meaning: Here, a man hostile to the Sages who mocks Rav Sheshet; the text does not name him.

berakhot-58a-12-14.note: Rabbi Sheila had a man flogged for having relations with a non-Jewish woman. The man told the king that a Jew was judging without royal authority, and Rabbi Sheila was summoned. He said the man had relations with a female donkey, and Elijah the prophet came, looking like a man, and testified. Told that such a man deserved death, Rabbi Sheila said Jews had no power to execute since their exile. While they deliberated he recited a verse and explained it as praise of God for granting earthly kingship; pleased, they gave him a staff and told him to judge. Leaving, the man asked if God does miracles for liars. Rabbi Sheila said gentiles are called donkeys, then saw the man was going to report this, declared him a pursuer, and struck him dead with the staff.
berakhot-58a-12-14.why: The Gemara has just told of Rav Sheshet, who said that royalty on earth is like royalty in heaven. Rabbi Sheila's praise of the king makes the same comparison, and afterward he expounds the verse that saved him.

people.name: Rabbi Sheila
people.about: A Sage who judged a Jewish man and was summoned by the king's officials.

people.name: Elijah the prophet
people.about: Appears as a man and testifies on Rabbi Sheila's behalf.

terms.meaning: In Jewish law, someone trying to kill another; the Torah's rule is that one may kill him first. Rabbi Sheila says the man seeks to have him killed.
A name for God.
Given to Rabbi Sheila by the officials as a sign of his license to judge.

berakhot-58b-1-3.note: Ulla and Rav Ḥisda were walking past the doorway of the house of Rav Ḥana bar Ḥanilai, and Rav Ḥisda groaned and sighed. Ulla reminded him of teachings that sighing breaks half, or even all, of the body. Rav Ḥisda said he could not help it: this house once had sixty cooks by day and sixty by night for anyone in need, four doors open to every direction, and grain scattered outside in drought years so the embarrassed could take it at night, and its owner never took his hand from his pocket so a poor man of good family would not be shamed by waiting. Now it had fallen in ruins. Ulla quoted Rabbi Yoḥanan that the houses of the righteous were decreed to be destroyed with the Temple and will be restored; seeing him still unconsoled, he said: it is enough for a servant to be like his master.
berakhot-58b-1-3.why: The Gemara has just taught that one who sees Jewish houses in ruins recites the blessing 'the true Judge'. This story shows two Sages facing one such ruined house.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: Walks with Rav Ḥisda and tries to console him.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Sighs at the sight of a ruined house he remembers as generous.

people.name: Rav Ḥana bar Ḥanilai
people.about: Owner of the house, famous for feeding the needy.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: A Sage whose teachings about sighing and ruined houses Ulla quotes.

terms.meaning: The Holy Temple in Jerusalem, God's house, which was destroyed; Ulla compares the ruined house to it.

berakhot-58b-6-6.note: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, met Rav Ḥanina, son of Rav Ika, on the road. They told him that on seeing him they had recited two blessings: the one for seeing a Sage, and 'Who has given us life'. He answered that he had regarded them as equal to six hundred thousand of Israel and recited three blessings, those two and 'Who knows all secrets'. They said: Are you all that clever? They fixed their gaze on him, and he died.
berakhot-58b-6-6.why: The Gemara has just taught that one who sees a friend after thirty days recites 'Who has given us life'. Here Sages use that blessing, with the blessing over Sages, on meeting a colleague.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Meets Rav Ḥanina on the road with Rav Huna.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Travels with Rav Pappa.

people.name: Rav Ḥanina, son of Rav Ika
people.about: The colleague they meet, who claims to have recited a third blessing over them.

terms.meaning: A blessing of thanks for reaching a special moment, said here on seeing a friend not seen for a while.
The blessing said on seeing a crowd of six hundred thousand Jews.

berakhot-59a-3-3.note: Rav Ketina was walking along the road when, at the entrance of a necromancer's house, an earthquake rumbled. He asked aloud whether the necromancer knew what this earthquake was. The necromancer called out: Ketina, Ketina, why would I not know? When God remembers His children suffering among the nations, He sheds two tears into the great sea, and the sound is heard from one end of the world to the other. That is an earthquake.
berakhot-59a-3-3.why: The mishna requires a blessing over zeva'ot, which Rav Ketina defines as earthquakes. Right after the story he calls the necromancer a liar, and the Gemara says he denied it only so people would not follow the necromancer.

people.name: Rav Ketina
people.about: A Sage who asks what an earthquake is and hears the necromancer's answer.

terms.meaning: Someone who claims to consult the dead.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses line by line.
A word in the mishna for a natural event over which one blesses God; Rav Ketina says it means an earthquake.

berakhot-60a-15-15.note: Hillel the Elder was coming along the road when he heard a scream in the city. He said: I am certain that it is not coming from my house. The Sages apply to him the verse 'He shall not be afraid of evil tidings; his heart is steadfast, trusting in the Lord', and Rava explains that the verse makes sense read from beginning to end or from end to beginning.
berakhot-60a-15-15.why: The mishna has just called it a vain prayer to ask, on hearing a scream, that it not be from one's own house. Hillel shows a different response: confidence instead of that prayer.

people.name: Hillel the Elder
people.about: A Sage who hears a scream and is sure it is not from his house.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who explains the verse applied to Hillel.

berakhot-60a-16-16.note: A student was walking behind Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, in the marketplace of Zion, and Rabbi Yishmael saw that he was afraid. He told him: You are a sinner, as it is written, 'The transgressors in Zion are afraid.' The student replied: Is it not written, 'Happy is the man that fears always'? Rabbi Yishmael answered that that verse is about matters of Torah.
berakhot-60a-16-16.why: The Gemara has just praised Hillel, whose trust in God left him unafraid of bad news. This story continues that theme and limits the verse praising constant fear to matters of Torah.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who rebukes a frightened student.

terms.meaning: Another name for Jerusalem.

berakhot-60a-17-17.note: Yehuda bar Natan was walking behind Rav Hamnuna and sighed. Rav Hamnuna said: Does this man want to bring suffering on himself? As it is written, 'For that which I did fear is come upon me.' Yehuda bar Natan answered: Is it not written, 'Happy is the man who fears always'? Rav Hamnuna replied that that verse is about matters of Torah.
berakhot-60a-17-17.why: This follows the story of the frightened student and Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei. It is a second case where a Sage rebukes a follower for fearing, and again the verse praising fear is limited to Torah.

people.name: Yehuda bar Natan
people.about: Walks behind Rav Hamnuna and sighs.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Sage who warns him that fear brings suffering.

berakhot-60a-26-26.note: Rabbi Abbahu went into a bathhouse, and its floor collapsed beneath him. A miracle happened: he stood on a pillar and saved one hundred and one men with one arm. He said: This is what Rav Aḥa meant.
berakhot-60a-26-26.why: Rav Aḥa has just taught that on leaving a bathhouse one thanks God for being saved from the fire. Rabbi Abbahu's rescue is offered as confirmation that such thanks are due.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage saved by a miracle when a bathhouse floor collapsed.

people.name: Rav Aḥa
people.about: A Sage whose teaching about thanks on leaving a bathhouse Rabbi Abbahu recalls.

terms.meaning: A public bath; the discussion treats entering one as a danger because of its fire.

berakhot-60b-11-12.note: Rabbi Akiva was traveling and came to a town where no one would give him lodging. He said: Everything God does is for the best, and slept in a field. He had a rooster, a donkey and a candle with him. The wind blew out the candle, a cat ate the rooster, and a lion ate the donkey, and he said again: Everything God does is for the best. That night an army came and took the town captive. He said to them: Didn't I tell you? Everything God does is for the best. The translation explains that he was spared because no light or animal gave away where he was.
berakhot-60b-11-12.why: The Gemara is bringing verses showing that one blesses God for bad things as well as good. Rav Huna, quoting Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Akiva, teaches that one should always say 'everything God does is for the best', and this incident is its example.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who keeps saying everything God does is for the best through a night of losses.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Reports the teaching that one should always say this.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages not included in the mishna, the main early collection of Jewish law.

berakhot-61b-5-9.note: When Rome decreed that Jews may not study Torah, Pappos ben Yehuda found Rabbi Akiva teaching it to public gatherings and asked if he feared the empire. Rabbi Akiva told a parable: a fox invited fish fleeing nets onto dry land, and they answered that if they feared in the water where they live, all the more where they would die; Torah is Israel's life. Soon both were jailed, and Pappos said Rabbi Akiva was fortunate to be held for Torah, while he was held for idle matters. As Rabbi Akiva was executed, his flesh raked with iron combs, he recited the Shema, telling his students he had long waited to fulfill 'with all your soul'. He died on the word 'One', and a heavenly voice praised him. The angels protested, God answered them, and a voice said he was destined for the World-to-Come.
berakhot-61b-5-9.why: The mishna and a baraita have just read 'with all your soul' as Rabbi Akiva did: love God even if He takes your soul. This story shows Rabbi Akiva living out that reading at his death.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who keeps teaching Torah under Roman decree and is executed.

people.name: Pappos ben Yehuda
people.about: Warns Rabbi Akiva about the empire and is later jailed with him.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who answers the angels' protest.

terms.meaning: The central Jewish declaration of faith, said daily: 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One.'
A voice from heaven that announces God's judgment.
The angels who serve before God.
The life after this world in which the righteous are rewarded.

berakhot-61b-15-15.note: In Rabba's bathroom the bricks were laid east and west, so that he would face north and south. Abaye moved them to north and south; Rabba came in, put them back and asked who was upsetting him, saying he followed Rabbi Akiva, who forbade facing east and west anywhere. In a separate account, Rabbi Akiva recalled following his teacher Rabbi Yehoshua into the bathroom and learning three things from watching him: face north or south, uncover yourself only when sitting, and wipe with the left hand. Ben Azzai asked whether he had been so bold with his teacher, and Rabbi Akiva answered: It is Torah, and I must learn.
berakhot-61b-15-15.why: The Gemara has just set out a dispute over which directions one may face when relieving oneself, with Rabbi Akiva forbidding east and west even outside the Land of Israel. Rabba follows his ruling, and Rabbi Akiva's own account shows where he learned it.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who insisted on the direction of his bathroom bricks.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Moves Rabba's bricks.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Learned bathroom practice by following his teacher.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's teacher.

people.name: Ben Azzai
people.about: Challenges Rabbi Akiva for watching his teacher so closely.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages not included in the mishna, the main early collection of Jewish law.

berakhot-62a-2-2.note: Rav Kahana went in and lay under Rav's bed. He heard Rav chatting and laughing with his wife and having relations with her. Rav Kahana said that Rav acted like one who had never eaten a cooked dish. Rav said: Kahana, you are here? Leave, this is not proper behavior. Rav Kahana answered: It is Torah, and I must learn.
berakhot-62a-2-2.why: The Gemara has just told of Rabbi Akiva and Ben Azzai following their teachers into the bathroom and defending it with 'It is Torah, and I must learn'. Rav Kahana uses the same words for an even more private intrusion.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Hides under Rav's bed to learn how he behaves.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage he watches, who tells him to leave.

terms.meaning: Rav's own name, which Rav Kahana uses here.

berakhot-62a-6-6.note: There was a bathroom in Tiberias where, when two people went in together, they were harmed, even by day. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi each went in alone and were not harmed. The Sages asked them: Aren't you afraid? They said they had a tradition: for the bathroom, modesty and silence; for suffering, silence and prayer.
berakhot-62a-6-6.why: Rabbi Tanḥum bar Ḥanilai has just said that one who is modest in the bathroom is saved from snakes, scorpions and demons. These two Sages, safe in a dangerous bathroom, show that protection at work.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Entered the dangerous bathroom alone and was not harmed.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: Entered the dangerous bathroom alone and was not harmed.

berakhot-62a-8-8.note: Before Rava became head of the yeshiva, his wife, the daughter of Rav Ḥisda, would rattle a nut in a copper vessel for him when he went to the bathroom. After he became head, she made a window for him and placed her hand on his head.
berakhot-62a-8-8.why: The Gemara is telling how people guarded against demons in the bathroom, as Abaye's mother did by raising a lamb to go with him. This is another such precaution, made greater once Rava held higher office.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage whose wife protected him in the bathroom.

people.name: The daughter of Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Rava's wife, who devised the protections.

terms.meaning: An academy of Torah study, led by a head who teaches the students.

berakhot-62a-14-14.note: A eulogizer came to speak before Rav Naḥman and said of the dead man that he was modest in his ways. Rav Naḥman said to him: Did you go into the bathroom with him, that you know whether he was modest or not? He cited a teaching that only one who is modest in the bathroom may be called modest.
berakhot-62a-14-14.why: The Gemara is discussing modesty when relieving oneself. Right afterward it explains Rav Naḥman's insistence: eulogizers are punished along with the dead for praising virtues the dead did not have.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: A Sage who challenges a eulogizer's praise of the dead.

terms.meaning: A person who speaks in praise of the dead at a funeral.
A teaching of the early Sages not included in the mishna, the main early collection of Jewish law.

berakhot-62b-3-3.note: Rav Safra was in a bathroom when Rabbi Abba came along and coughed by the door. Rav Safra said: Enter, master. When he came out, Rabbi Abba rebuked him: You have never gone to Seir, yet you have learned the ways of Seir? He cited the teaching about the Temple's bathroom of honor, where a locked door meant someone was inside and an open one meant no one was, which shows that speaking in the bathroom is not proper.
berakhot-62b-3-3.why: The Gemara is gathering rules of modesty in the bathroom. Right afterward it defends Rav Safra: he spoke because making Rabbi Abba wait could endanger his health.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Was in the bathroom and invited Rabbi Abba in.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Rebukes Rav Safra for speaking in the bathroom.

terms.meaning: The land of the Edomites, who the translation says were not strict about modesty.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses line by line.
The Holy Temple in Jerusalem.

berakhot-62b-5-5.note: Rabbi Elazar went into a bathroom, and a Roman came and pushed him out. Rabbi Elazar got up and left. A serpent then came and ripped out the Roman's intestines. Rabbi Elazar applied a verse to him, "Therefore I will give man for you," reading the Hebrew word for "man" (adam) as "Edom," a name the Sages used for Rome.
berakhot-62b-5-5.why: The Gemara is gathering teachings and incidents about conduct and modesty in the bathroom; this one follows the story of Rav Safra and Rabbi Abba at a bathroom door, and is followed by a lesson drawn from Saul's modesty in the cave.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who was pushed out of a bathroom by a Roman, and who applied a verse to the Roman's death.

terms.meaning: The nation descended from Esau. The Sages used the name as a code word for Rome, which is why Rabbi Elazar rereads "adam" (man) as "Edom" (a Roman).

berakhot-63a-22-26.note: Rav Safra reports a story Rabbi Abbahu used to tell. Hanina, nephew of Rabbi Yehoshua, went to Babylonia and began fixing the calendar there, a task reserved for the Land of Israel. The Sages of Israel sent two scholars after him. At first he praised them publicly, but when they kept overturning his rulings he called them worthless; they answered that he could not tear down what he had built up. Their reason: he was fixing the calendar outside the Land. He cited Rabbi Akiva's example and his own stature, but they replied that the young students he left behind had grown into horned goats, and that he must obey or be ostracized. If the Babylonian Jews refused, they should declare they had no portion in the God of Israel. The whole people burst into tears and said they did.
berakhot-63a-22-26.why: Right after the story the Gemara asks why the Sages of Israel went to such lengths, and answers with the verse "For out of Zion shall go forth the Torah"; it then asks how the visitors were allowed to overturn another Sage's rulings.

people.name: Hanina
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehoshua's brother; he went to Babylonia and fixed the calendar there.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: The Sage who used to tell this story, as Rav Safra reports.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: The Sage who passes on Rabbi Abbahu's account.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Keifar
people.about: One of the two scholars the Sages of Israel sent after Hanina.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: An earlier Sage whom Hanina cites as having also fixed the calendar outside the Land of Israel.

terms.meaning: Fixing the Jewish calendar: deciding when a new month begins and when to add a leap month to a year. The law reserves this authority for the Land of Israel.
Placed under a ban by the Sages, so that the community keeps its distance from the person until he submits.
The Jewish communities living outside the Land of Israel; here, Babylonia.

berakhot-64a-2-4.note: Rav Yosef was called "Sinai" for his vast knowledge, and Rabba "one who uproots mountains" for his sharpness. When one of them had to be chosen to head the yeshiva, they asked the Sages of the Land of Israel which came first, and were told "Sinai," since everyone needs the owner of the wheat. Rav Yosef still declined, because Chaldean astrologers had told him he would preside for only two years. Rabba presided for twenty-two years and then Rav Yosef for two and a half. All the years Rabba led, Rav Yosef did not even summon a bloodletter to his home.
berakhot-64a-2-4.why: Rabbi Avin HaLevi has just taught that one who yields to the moment finds the moment yields to him; the Gemara brings Rav Yosef, who gave up the post and still received it later, as the proof.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Called "Sinai" for his erudition; offered the headship of the yeshiva, he declined it.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Called "one who uproots mountains" for his sharpness; he headed the yeshiva for twenty-two years.

terms.meaning: An academy of Torah study; its head was the leading authority of the community of scholars.
Stargazers from Babylonia whose predictions were widely consulted; here they foretold the length of Rav Yosef's tenure.
A practitioner who drew blood as a medical treatment. Rav Yosef went to the bloodletter rather than having him come to his home, so as not to act like a man in authority.
